boundaries against literal strings before any sweep is trusted to report an
absence. That self-test earned itself on its first run: under `grep -i` the
camelCase class `[a-z0-9_]Board` folds to `[a-z0-9_]board` and matches the
"hboard" inside "dashboard" — a boundary silently destroyed by the flag meant
to make the check more thorough. The sweeps now run case-sensitive and carry
their casing in the pattern.

payload.title: Rebuild project monitor and project status around tasks, not sessions
payload.description: Rebuild both views around tasks rather than sessions, per Mike's specification on 2026-09-15 with the monitor open in front of him. Three lists in one pane, no separators: urgent (untruncated), then epics in now/next (untruncated), then everything else in now/next — the only truncated list, taking whatever pane height remains. All reverse-chronological, with --sort taking updated (default) or id. Each task appears once, in the highest list it qualifies for. project status truncates nothing at all and gains --later. Rows reuse session status rendering minus the age column and minus the session-relative glyphs, keeping the action and phase glyphs; sessions are still consulted so a live session shows as a different glyph, but no session is ever a row. Removes the seven-rank grouping, the per-rank cap, --limit/--no-limit and --all. Interim by intent: a scrolling TUI is expected to replace it.
payload.plan:
# Plan — rebuild project monitor and project status around tasks

Specified by Mike in conversation on 2026-09-15, with `project monitor` open in
front of him. This replaces the display E-1976 shipped; it is not a tweak to it.

Explicitly an interim shape. Mike expects to replace it with a scrolling TUI
before long, and wants to live with this one to learn what he actually needs.
Build what is specified here and stop; do not optimise past it.

## The shape

One tmux pane holds the whole of `project monitor`, with the CLI pane beneath it
(the existing two-pane layout, unchanged). Inside that pane, THREE lists, in this
order, with NO separator rows and no headers between them:

1. **urgent** — `phase = 'urgent'`, non-terminal. UNTRUNCATED.
2. **epics** — `type = epic`, `phase IN ('now','next')`, non-terminal.
   UNTRUNCATED.
3. **everything else** — non-epic, `phase IN ('now','next')`, non-terminal.
   The ONLY truncated list: it takes whatever pane height remains, and grows
   when the user grows the terminal.

Each task appears ONCE, in the highest list it qualifies for: an urgent epic is
in list 1, never also in list 2; an epic is never in list 3.

Separators are unnecessary because the rows identify themselves — list 1 carries
the urgent phase glyph, list 2 carries the epic type letter. Mike may revisit
this; do not add separators pre-emptively.

## Ordering

All three lists sort reverse-chronologically.

`--sort` on BOTH `project monitor` and `project status`, taking `updated`
(default) or `id`. Mike was undecided between them and wants to try both in use,
which is the flag's whole purpose — do not pick one and drop the other.

## `project status` does not truncate

Not the third list, not anything. It is the surface for seeing everything,
including what the monitor cannot fit, and Mike expects to pipe it through grep
routinely to find tasks the monitor is not showing.

`--later` shows ONLY `phase = 'later'` tasks — the phase the other views exclude.

## Rows

Reuse `session status`'s row rendering. It is well optimised for an experienced
reader and there is no reason to invent a second format; share the code.

Changes for this context:

- **Drop the time/age column.** It is not useful here, and — the reason that
  matters more — it changes every tick, so the frame differs on every repaint and
  the pane moves constantly in the corner of the eye. Removing it makes motion
  mean something: the pane only redraws when the row set actually changes.
- **Drop the session-relative glyphs**: `●` (this session's task), `↑` (parent),
  `↩` (from/spawner). They describe a viewing session, and there is none here.
- **Keep the action glyph.** E-1976's error was GROUPING by it, not showing it.
- **Keep the phase glyph on every row**, including in the urgent list where it is
  technically redundant — for vertical alignment, and because it is what the eye
  is used to.
- Keep the type letter, the id, and the title.

## Sessions are consulted, never displayed

No session appears as a row. But a task's row DOES reflect whether a live session
is on it: `⟳` for `underway` with a live session, `◷` for `underway` without —
the distinction `session status` already draws, and the only signal that claimed
work has stalled.

E-2091's `prompted` state extends this naturally: a task whose live session is
blocked on a permission prompt should wear the `⚠` glyph rather than `⟳`, since
that is the same fact at a higher urgency. STATED EXPLICITLY so it can be
rejected: it follows from "the row reflects a live session" plus the existing
glyph vocabulary, but Mike did not say it in as many words.

## What is removed

- **All session rows**, and with them the "sessions with no task" list that
  prompted this redesign. They were unactionable — three such rows led to
  "Session NNN has no reachable tmux pane" when followed.
- **Idle-session reporting.** tmux window tabs already carry it. Out of scope
  now; Mike may revisit when a TUI can do more.
- **The seven-rank classification as a grouping mechanism** (`waiting`, `verify`,
  `read`, `review`, `orphan`, `idle`, `doing`). The glyphs survive on rows; the
  grouping does not. There is no ordering among statuses that says one matters
  more than another — they are all points in one workflow.
- **The per-rank cap and its fair-share allocation.** One list truncates, by pane
  height alone.
- **`--limit` / `--no-limit`.** Nothing is count-capped any more. This leaves
  `rowcap.limit_options_for` with no caller; remove it too if so, rather than
  leaving a factory nothing builds from.
- **`--all`.** Its meaning was "also include `ready`", which is now included by
  default as a non-terminal status.

Keep `--json` and the fault badge as they are.

## Status filtering was considered and rejected

Measured while planning: list 3 holds 295 tasks for this project — 127
`unplanned`, 92 `submitted`, 38 `unverified`, 25 `ready`, 13 `underway`.

The obvious move is to filter to statuses needing the user specifically. Mike
rejected it (2026-09-15): `session status` carries the per-session detail, this
is the high-level view, and no status is inherently more important than another
because they are all part of one workflow. `unplanned` and `ready` are both
needed now — they may matter less once auto-spawn and auto-planning exist, which
is a reason to revisit later and not to filter now.

The pane running out of room is not a defect to design around. It is the pressure
that gets work demoted to `later`, the same way 20 untruncated epics is the
pressure that gets epics demoted.

## Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-<id>/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit gate: `internal/projectstatuscmd`, `internal/monitor`, and the
   Python suite.
2. The three lists, in order, against a seeded database: an urgent task, an
   urgent epic, a now epic, a next epic, and non-epic tasks across the
   non-terminal statuses. Assert the order and that each task appears exactly
   once.
3. Untruncated means untruncated: seed more urgent tasks and more epics than fit
   a small `--rows` budget and assert every one renders.
4. Only list 3 truncates, and by height: the same row set at two `--rows` values
   yields more list-3 rows at the larger one, with lists 1 and 2 unchanged.
5. `--sort id` and `--sort updated` produce different orders on a fixture built
   so they must (an old task updated recently).
6. `project status` truncates nothing at any `--rows` value, and `--later` shows
   only `later` tasks.
7. No row renders a session: no `ES-` id, and no `●`/`↑`/`↩` glyph, on any
   fixture.
8. A task held by a live session renders `⟳` and the same task with no live
   session renders `◷`.
9. No age column: two renders of an unchanged row set, taken a second apart, are
   byte-identical. This is the repaint-motion property, and asserting it on the
   frame is what keeps it from regressing when a future column carries a clock.

fields.title: Explore how project monitor gets its own window, and what verb opens it
fields.description: Opening endless project monitor in its own window requires remembering a flag on a subcommand (--tmux), the bare verb does something else (renders in the current pane), and with the flag it switch-clients the caller, replacing a live tmux session's windows with the monitor. What it wants is its own terminal window. Explore the verb (Mike's sketch: a top-level 'endless monitor') and a pluggable launcher: a config setting names the terminal, the setting selects a script, Endless ships scripts for terminals people ask for and users can add their own. Cover the script's contract, what happens with no window system or no matching script, and whether the launcher belongs to project monitor or is shared with task spawn, which already opens tmux windows. The display half was settled separately and is now E-2156.
fields.plan:
# Seed / framing

`endless project monitor --tmux` is how `project monitor` opens today, and
three things are wrong with it.

**The flag is unintuitive.** `project monitor` is a standing surface you open once and
leave. Reaching it requires remembering a flag on a subcommand, and the bare
verb does something different (renders in the current pane). Mike's sketch:
`endless monitor` doing what `project monitor --tmux` does now.

**It hijacks a live session.** Run with `--tmux` from inside an attached tmux
session, it `switch-client`s the caller to the monitor session — replacing the
user's windows with `project monitor`. Recoverable, but it takes over a workspace the
user did not offer.

**There is no way to open it somewhere new.** What `project monitor` actually wants is
its own terminal window, not a tmux session grafted onto the caller's client.
`open -a Terminal` was tried as a proof of concept and restarted Terminal.app,
dropping both tmux sessions — not viable.

# What to explore

- What the verb should be, and what it does when run bare versus with a target.
  Is `endless monitor` a new top-level verb, an alias, or a replacement?
- How a board gets its own window without commandeering the caller's. On macOS
  with Terminal.app an `osascript` can open a window and run a command in it.
  What is the equivalent for iTerm2, WezTerm, Ghostty, kitty, Alacritty, tmux
  alone, a bare TTY, and a remote session over SSH?
- Mike's proposal: a pluggable launcher. A config setting names the terminal,
  the setting selects a script, Endless ships scripts for the terminals people
  ask for, and a user can drop in their own. What is the script's contract —
  what is it given, what must it guarantee, what does Endless do when it fails
  or when no script matches?
- Whether the launcher belongs to `project monitor` at all, or is general: `task spawn`
  already builds a tmux window, and a second thing that opens terminals would
  be two mechanisms for one job.
- What happens with no window system: SSH, a CI shell, a detached daemon. The
  board must still be reachable, and refusing to open is a legitimate answer if
  it says what to run instead.
- Whether the tmux path stays at all once a real window launcher exists, or
  becomes one script among several.

# Constraints

Judge as a product, not as this machine (PRODUCT). The design cannot assume
macOS, cannot assume Terminal.app, cannot assume tmux, and must degrade sensibly
for someone on a fresh install in a single terminal. Say explicitly what it does
in `self_dev` mode versus for a project merely using Endless as a tool.

The current `--tmux` behaviour is a shipped bug, not merely a design smell: a
session-hijack is worth fixing regardless of where this lands.



# Already settled, and out of scope here

The display half of this brainstorm was run with Mike on 2026-09-15 and
resolved into E-2156. What `project monitor` shows, how it ranks, what a row
carries and what truncates are decided; do not reopen them here. This task is
now only about the verb that opens it and the window it opens into.

payload.title: The goose baseline is the current schema; prior change files are discarded, not converted
payload.description: Migration 00001 is the CURRENT schema, generated from the live shape, rather than a replay of the 34 files under internal/schema/changes/. Those were written to be applied once at land, to one database, and are not a schema history: on the real ledger _schema_version holds 46 rows (12 legacy vNN- names plus 34 change basenames) against 34 files on disk, and the sets disagree in BOTH directions -- e-1542-session-gates is on disk and was never applied, e-1653-migrate-status-data is applied and its file is gone. Several files rebuild tables that later files rebuild again, so replaying them reconstructs historical schemas nobody needs to reach a state schema.sql already describes. Accepted cost: no database older than the baseline can be migrated forward. Only one real database exists and it is current; sandboxes are rebuilt, and a worktree predating the baseline rebases. Distinct from ED-1566 (demotes schema.sql, silent on the change files) and ED-1565 (chooses goose, not what it starts from).

fields.description: The errors surface has seven problems, found while reading two real incidents. 'show' lists rather than showing one item, and there is no detail view for a single error even though the listing truncates summaries. The default listing omits the project, so 'errors show' printed 'no errors' inside one project while the status line reported one error and one warning from another -- two surfaces flatly disagreeing. The listing wraps and spends ten characters spelling out severities that an icon conveys, in both the list and the status line. ERR-0001 carries an ERR prefix while being severity warning. Nothing anywhere tells a user how to resolve anything, though docs/errors.md already carries a remedy per code. And the one-line notification those status views append is called a 'badge' throughout -- a name a session coined and later sessions treated as settled vocabulary; Mike finds it unintuitive and wants 'notification row'. Expect many landings under this id rather than a task per tweak.
fields.analysis:
## Expect many landings, not many tasks

Mike will iterate on this layout repeatedly. Land it, look at it, adjust, land
again — under THIS task id rather than filing a new task per tweak. The task is
the surface, not any one revision of it. Do not close it because one pass shipped.

## What is wrong today

Observed 2026-09-15 on a machine with two open incidents.

**1. `show` is the wrong verb.** It lists. `show` elsewhere in the CLI means "one
item, in detail" (`task show`, `decision show`). This should be `errors list`,
leaving `errors show <id>` free to mean what `show` means everywhere else.

**2. `errors show <id>` has nothing to show.** There is no detail view. The
listing truncates the summary mid-word with an ellipsis and there is nowhere to
go for the rest.

**3. The listing does not say which project caused it.** Default scope is the
current project, and the PROJECT column appears only under `--all-projects`. That
produced a flat contradiction: `endless errors show` printed "no errors" from
inside the endless project while the status line simultaneously reported
`1 error, 1 warning`, because both incidents belonged to a different project.
Two surfaces disagreeing about whether anything is wrong is worse than either
answer alone.

**4. It wraps, and wastes the width it has.** SEVERITY spells out "warning" and
"error" in full, and the status line spells out "1 error, 1 warning". Icons carry
the same distinction in one column instead of ten, in both places. Reclaim the
width for the summary, which is the part being truncated.

**5. A warning carries an ERR- code.** `ERR-0001` is severity warning. Either the
prefix should follow severity (`WARN-0001`) or the prefix should be severity-
neutral; today it states one thing and means another.

**6. Nothing says how to resolve any of it.** The footer explains how to DISMISS
an incident and is careful to say dismissing is not a retry — but the incident
itself carries no remedy. `docs/errors.md` has a "What to do" section for every
code, and the listing never points at it. A user reading the list learns that
something is wrong and not one thing about fixing it.

**7. "Badge" is a name nobody chose.** The one-line notification that
`session status`, `session monitor`, `project status` and `project monitor`
append below their rows is called a "badge" everywhere: the package is
`internal/faultbadge`, and docs/guide/reference.md teaches the word. Asked
2026-09-16 what it referred to, Mike: "That is completely unintuitive to me.
'Notification row' makes more sense here."

It survived because a session coined it and later sessions cited that coinage as
though it were settled product vocabulary — the term appears nowhere Mike wrote
it. A name that exists only in text Claude produced is unratified, however many
files carry it.

The rename spans the package name, the comments throughout it, docs/errors.md,
docs/guide/reference.md, and the guide's errors section: mechanical but wide.
Folded here on Mike's direction (surfaced during E-2151) rather than filed
separately, because this task owns the surface and item 4 already touches the
same row. It should still land as its own pass rather than mixed into a
functional one.

## Not in scope

The per-code remedy TEXT already exists in docs/errors.md and is asserted complete
by the faults package's own tests. This task surfaces it; it does not rewrite it.

fields.plan:
`docs/guide/orchestration.md` ("A verify suite is a land-time gate, not a
standing regression suite") states three prohibitions:

- Don't run another task's already-landed verify suite.
- Don't edit a landed task's verify suite.
- Coverage that must survive belongs in the project's own test suite.

The rule is documented and was still violated three times in one session
(E-1901), including by a session whose handoff explicitly named
`endless guide orchestration`. It was then violated twice more in E-1889, by a
session that had read the same principle in its own task's analysis field on
its first tool call. Documentation is the wrong layer: a rule that must be read
gets skipped, and the skip does not feel like a violation — running an existing,
runnable-looking script feels like diligence.

Put the enforcement where the act happens, in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go`,
following the `blockPlanFileWriteIfApplicable` precedent already in that file
(same shape, same class of problem: a path that must not be hand-edited).

## Both suite forms, from day one

A suite exists in two forms and the guard must know both, or it goes blind
exactly when the project migrates:

| Form | Path | Run by |
|------|------|--------|
| script (current) | `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` | `./tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` |
| manifest (settled destination) | `.endless/tasks/e-<n>/verify.toml` | `endless task verify <id>` |

Both paths write the id lowercase. The manifest directories were uppercase
until they were renamed and `verify.Discover` was taught to compare ids
normalized (`verify.NormalizeTaskID`); the manifest's own `task` field remains
the canonical `E-NNNN` display form. Because an uppercase directory still
resolves, the id-extraction predicate here must accept either casing rather
than assuming the lowercase convention holds on disk.

Building the manifest arm now is not speculation. Two manifests already exist
and `endless task verify` already discovers and runs them. Shipping a
script-only guard would mean re-opening this task the moment the migration
lands — the precise failure mode this task exists to prevent.

### What must NOT be blocked

- **`.endless/verify.toml` at the project root.** Same filename, one level up,
  and it is not a per-task suite — it carries shared `setup`/`teardown`/`seed`/
  `needs` composing beneath every task manifest. The predicate keys on the
  `.endless/tasks/<id>/` segment, not on the basename.
- **The tests a manifest points AT.** A manifest is a pointer, never a
  re-description: its `[[check]]` entries select native `gotest`/`pytest` tests
  living in `internal/...` and `tests/...`. Those are the project's durable
  suite and must stay freely editable forever. Blocking the manifest must not
  leak into blocking what it names — which is the whole reason the durable-test
  half of the prohibition works.

## Arm 1 — refuse the EDIT (the more damaging violation)

`PreToolUse` on Write/Edit/NotebookEdit: refuse a target matching either suite
form when task NNNN has landed AND is not this session's active task.

This is the arm that matters most. In E-1901 the suites were edited via Edit
without ever being run, so any guard living inside the script itself was inert.
Retrofitting the target string of a landed suite rewrites the record of what was
true when that task landed. In E-1889 the motive was more specific and worth
naming, because it will recur: the session's own change broke a landed suite's
assertion, and it edited the suite to keep it green. That is the failure this
arm must catch — the edit feels like fixing a break, not like falsifying a
record.

## Arm 2 — refuse the RUN

Same handler, Bash tool. ONE invocation shape, refused for a landed, non-active
task: direct execution of a suite script (any of `./x`, `bash x`, `sh x`, an
absolute path).

A failure from a landed suite is meaningless by design, and acting on one
produces exactly the non-problem work E-1909 and E-1910 were (both declined).

### Amended (E-2023 planning, 2026-08-27): the runner clause is dropped

This arm originally also refused `endless task verify <id>` and the `just verify
<id>` wrapper. That clause is REMOVED, because E-2023 puts the same refusal
inside the runner itself, where the task id is known for certain.

The hook and the command are not equally good places for this check, and the
difference decides it. The hook matches a COMMAND STRING and infers the target
from it, so it can refuse an invocation that was never going to run a suite and
miss one spelled a way the pattern did not anticipate — false positives and
false negatives, both. The command already holds the resolved id as an argument;
it cannot be wrong about what it is being asked to verify. With the check in the
command there is no reason to also guess at it in the hook, and one rule
implemented twice against the same landed-ness lookup is a rule that can drift.

Direct execution stays here precisely because it is the case the command cannot
see: nothing routes through the runner, so nothing else is watching.

E-2090 narrows what that has to cover: it prepends a shared `_guard.sh` to every
existing suite script, so a direct run refuses from inside the file itself. Arm 2
is nevertheless RETAINED (Mike, 2026-08-27) as a backstop for the two cases an
in-file guard cannot reach — a suite checked out from a commit predating the
guard, and one hand-authored without it. It is no longer the only guard for those
~200 scripts, and after E-2090 it should be expected to fire rarely; that is the
shape of a backstop, not evidence it is unnecessary.

The interlock is worth naming, because it runs the other way too: the guard lives
INSIDE the file it guards, so Arm 1 — refusing edits to a landed suite — is what
stops the guard line being deleted. Neither arm makes the other redundant.

Note also that E-2023 relocates suites to `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.sh`. The
path table above records what was true when this plan was written; whichever task
lands second reconciles. The move SIMPLIFIES this arm — both suite forms then sit
under the single `.endless/tasks/<id>/` segment the predicate already keys on for
manifests.

## Landed-ness test

`session-query task-report --id N` already returns a `landed` bool; reuse it
rather than adding a second notion of landed-ness. Carve out the session's own
active task so the live, pre-land gate still runs and can still be authored.

A reopened task (`revisit`, per E-1889) is once again the session's active task,
so the carve-out restores its suite to writable and runnable without a special
case — reopening genuinely does put the task back in its pre-land window.

## Why no directory move, and no per-script retrofit

Moving `tests/tasks/` → `verify/tasks/` was considered and rejected: 123 task
rows and 141 commit messages embed the current path, all of them immutable
records, and `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml` is already the settled
destination as the runner matures — a move would churn the script form on its
way out. A rename also would not have prevented the violation: the scripts were
run because they existed and looked runnable, not because of the directory name.

Because the guard lives in the hook, NO existing suite is touched and every
landed suite of either form is covered the moment it ships. That is the point: a
per-script guard could only be added by editing landed suites, which is the
prohibition itself.

## Honest limits

- This cannot stop an agent from FILING a task about a landed suite — that is a
  judgment call no path pattern catches. E-1909/E-1910's decline reasons are the
  record for that case.
- It cannot stop a run laundered through an indirection the Bash matcher does
  not see (a wrapper script, `xargs`, a shell function). Arm 2 is a guardrail
  against the reflex, not a sandbox; Arm 1 is the arm that must be airtight.

## Verification

Unit tests on the pure predicate, covering both forms:

- path regex matches `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` and
  `.endless/tasks/e-<n>/verify.toml`, in either casing (uppercase suite dirs
  still resolve), and not their neighbours;
- the project-root `.endless/verify.toml` is NOT matched;
- a path named by a manifest's `[[check]]` (e.g. `internal/monitor/x_test.go`)
  is NOT matched;
- landed + non-active → block; landed + active → allow; unlanded → allow;
- run-arm command parsing: the three script invocation shapes and
  `endless task verify <id>` / `just verify <id>` block; bare
  `endless task verify` allows;
- the block-response shape.

Those tests are the DURABLE deliverable and live in the Go suite beside the
handler. They are the coverage that has to outlive this task, so they do not
depend on the acceptance suite below existing.

### This task's own acceptance suite

Author it as a **script**:

    tests/tasks/e-1916-verify.sh

**Do NOT author a `.endless/tasks/e-1916/verify.toml`.** The manifest form is
not yet the norm and will not be until the E-1596 epic lands. As of this
writing E-1596 still has open children — E-1606, E-1608, E-1609, E-1614,
E-1623, E-1692, E-1792, E-1793 — including E-1623, which is the task that
retrofits the existing `tests/tasks/*.sh` suites onto the shared harness. Until
that epic closes, the script IS the form.

This is worth stating loudly because every surface an agent checks argues the
opposite, and two sessions have now reached the wrong conclusion from it:

- `endless task verify --help` reads as fully operational and tells you to run
  it before `task confirm`/`task assume`;
- two manifests exist on disk and the command really does run them;
- six E-1596 children sit at `assumed`, which reads as done.

(The guide used to be the loudest of these signals — it documented the manifest
with a full schema. That documentation has since been removed, because the
guide is product documentation for every project using Endless and must not
describe a form that has not shipped.)

All true, and none of it means the migration has happened. A working runner
with two exemplar suites is not a convention; E-1596 closing is.

Once this task lands, its own suite falls under the guard it ships. That is
correct and is worth checking by hand once: after landing, an attempt to edit
or run `tests/tasks/e-1916-verify.sh` from a session that does not hold E-1916
must be refused by the very hook this task added.

Surfaced by E-1901, where all three prohibitions were violated in sequence:
six landed suites run, three edited (reverted in 54df9715), and two non-problem
tasks filed and declined. Re-confirmed by E-1889, where two landed suites were
edited (reverted in that branch before landing) and four were run as a standing
regression gate.









---

## Reconciled at implementation (2026-09-16)

The plan was written before E-2023 and E-2090 landed. Three things it left
open are now settled, and one small thing grew:

**The script form moved, so there is one path predicate, not two.** E-2023
retired `tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh`; nothing is tracked under `tests/tasks/`
any more, and both suite forms now sit under `.endless/tasks/<id>/`. The plan
said whichever task landed second reconciles, so the legacy arm is not built.
The predicate keys on the `<suites-dir>/e-NNNN/` SEGMENT and therefore covers
everything in a suite directory, fixtures and helpers included — not just
`verify.sh` and `verify.toml`.

**The suites directory is read from `verify.SuitesDir`, never spelled.** Both
matchers are built from that constant, so a project whose suites live elsewhere
moves this gate with them rather than being guarded at a path it does not use.

**Ownership has one more source in the hook than in the runner.**
`monitor.SuiteOwnershipFor` supplies landed-ness (the same `task_landings`
lookup E-2023 uses, so the two cannot drift) and the two caller-tasks it can
resolve from the environment and the checkout. The hook adds the one only a
hook has: the session id Claude Code hands it, whose claimed task is the
session's own declaration. The union is the fail-open direction.

**Folded in, beyond the plan:**

- `monitor.taskReportFacts` now reads landed-ness through `taskHasLanded`
  instead of its own copy of the same query — the plan's "one notion of
  landed-ness", applied to the third copy of it in the package.
- `docs/guide/orchestration.md` names the new enforcement on both prohibitions.

  who refuses an EDIT; after this task both are refused, and a reader who gets
  blocked looks there.

and before `enforceWorktreeGate`, for the reason the plan-file gate sits there:
the suite-specific refusal must arrive ahead of the worktree gate's generic
"edits in main". Arm 2 sits among the registered-project Bash gates rather than
with the unconditional ones — an unregistered project has no landings to
protect, so the gate has nothing to say there and costs no database read.

Implements ED-1571, the one part of E-1944's outcome that was decided and never
filed.

Under ED-1567 a CANDIDATE binary may never migrate the real ledger. But
`_resolve_land_endless_go` in src/endless/worktree_cmd.py hands a self_dev land

choice: "the only binary whose embedded schema/enums match the just-written rows
is the worktree's own build — never the not-yet-refreshed global." That binary is
a candidate by `candidateBuild()`'s definition — its path carries the worktree
marker.

own migration: the installed one does not carry it, the worktree one is not
allowed to run it. That is why this exists, and it is why it blocks E-2020 rather
than following it.

migration set and nothing else. It performs migration steps in FULL — DDL plus
the DML those migrations define: enum seed rows, backfills, the INSERT ... SELECT

hook, never runs a task command, never touches business data outside a
migration. That exclusion is what makes it immune to the
binary-expects-a-schema failure, because it has no expectations beyond the
migrations it carries.

ordering: after the ff-merge, before `_record_landing`) instead of calling
`endless db apply-change` with the worktree binary.

Scope is self_dev ONLY. Every other project has one installed binary and no land
at all, so it carries and applies its own migrations under ED-1570; no separate
executable exists there, and nothing in this task may assume one does.

Two things to settle while planning, not now:
- `_record_landing` still runs on the worktree binary for the same E-1664
  reason, against a ledger this executable just migrated. Whether that remains
  correct under ED-1570's exact-agreement rule needs an answer.

  executable replaces that usage, E-1709's rebuild may be serving only

# Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-2088/`, run only through the runner — `just verify E-2088` or
`endless task verify E-2088`. Never executed directly: `_guard.sh` refuses that,
and a suite exercising land-time migration against your real `HOME` is precisely
the run that must not happen.

Shape: a `verify.toml` whose first `[[check]]` is a `gotest` runner over the
executable's unit tests — the fail-fast half — plus a `verify.sh` driving a land
end-to-end. The script sources `_harness.sh`, opens with the DO-NOT-EDIT header
naming E-2088, uses `section` / `assert_eq` / `assert_contains`, and calls
`summary` last; shipped fixtures are read from `$ENDLESS_VERIFY_DIR`.

The runner's temp `HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` are what make it safe to run a
real migration, so nothing here passes `--config-dir`.

1. The executable applies a migration end to end against a throwaway database:
   version before, version after, and the DML the migration defines actually ran
   (seed rows present, backfill applied), not just the DDL.
2. It refuses to do anything that is not a migration — assert the binary exposes
   no hook, task, or query surface, since "it never serves a hook" is the

3. `worktree land` invokes it at E-1941's apply step, between the ff-merge and

   message telling the operator to re-run rather than restore.
4. Landing a branch with no migration does not build or invoke it.
5. In a non-self_dev project no such executable exists and the installed binary
   applies its own migrations under ED-1570 — assert the self_dev-only scope
   rather than assuming it.
6. The worktree binary is still what `_record_landing` runs, against the ledger
   this executable just migrated. Assert that pairing works, because it is the
   half of E-1664 that survives E-2088 and nothing else covers it.

Coverage that must outlive the land is mirrored into the durable Go suite —
assertion 2's "no application surface" check in particular, since it is a
property of the build that would otherwise erode silently.

# What this grew to include

Three things larger than the task row described, folded in because each was
cheaper to do than to file and none of them widens the land's blast radius.

## internal/dbcontext — extracted, not duplicated

The executable needed to know where the database lives, and that answer lived
inside `internal/monitor`. Importing monitor for one path join would have put
the entire application — the schema-applying `monitor.DB()` above all — into a
binary whose only claim to safety is that it carries nothing but migrations, and
would have made the "no application surface" assertion a statement about the
command line rather than about the build.

So the resolution moved into a leaf package (`ConfigDir`, `DBPath`,
`ConsumeConfigDirFlag`) and `internal/monitor` delegates to it, keeping its own
routing — the hook's main pin, cwd sandbox self-detection, the explicit-context
gate — layered on top. One definition, two callers, and the executable's
dependency graph became an assertable property: a durable Go test reads
`go list -deps ./cmd/endless-migrate` against an ALLOWLIST of exactly
`dbcontext` + `schemachange` + the cmd itself, so any future import of an
application package fails a test rather than quietly undoing ED-1571.

The executable deliberately does NOT self-detect a worktree sandbox from cwd.
That is right for an application surface and wrong for a migration: a tool that
rewrites a schema resolves its target from what the caller named, never from
where it happens to be standing.

## internal/schemachange — one definition of applying a change

Rather than a second copy of the apply-and-record logic inside the new
executable, `runApplyChange` moved out of `internal/eventcmd` into
`internal/schemachange`, which takes an open handle and never opens a database
itself. The two applying programs now differ ONLY in how they opened one:
`endless-go event apply-change` through the application's connect, the migration
executable through a direct file open. That difference IS ED-1571, so it is the
only difference left in the code.

`internal/schema/changes/runner` (the helper a `.go` change imports) was pointed
at the same two packages, so a compiled change script links the migration
machinery and no application either. Same answer, same reason.

## E-1941's durable land tests were updated, not bypassed

`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` asserted the land's call order as
rebuild → backup → apply → record and monkeypatched
`event_bridge.apply_change` to do it. The apply is no longer that call, so the
module was updated to the real sequence — rebuild → build-migrate → backup →
apply → record — with both builds asserted to happen while base is still
behind. That module is the single definition of the land's ordering; leaving it
patched around a stale call would have left the ordering unasserted.

# Where the build sits, and why it is not exactly "at the apply step"

The task row says the land "builds and invokes it at the existing apply step".
The INVOKE is exactly there — between the ff-merge and `_record_landing`,
E-1941's window, unchanged. The BUILD is one step earlier, at 4.6: after the
change list is known (so a land with no migration builds nothing, which is what
makes its absence testable) and before the ff-merge, for the reason E-1941 gave
for the endless-go rebuild it sits beside — "a broken build aborts while main
and the DB are untouched, strictly safer". A tree that cannot compile its own
migration tool should not get as far as advancing base.

# The two questions the plan left open, answered

`_record_landing` KEEPS running the worktree's endless-go, and the split is the
point. Applying is forbidden to an unlanded build; recording is a DATA write,
which an unlanded build has always been allowed to make against the real
database, and it is the write whose enum constants must agree with the rows the
migration just inserted. The verification suite asserts that pairing end to end:
the executable migrates a ledger-shaped database, then the application's
connect — schema.sql plus all four fail-closed integrity gates — opens it and
honours the marker the other program wrote.

E-1709's pre-land rebuild therefore still has a consumer. After ED-1571 it
serves `_record_landing` and the pre-apply backup rather than the apply, and
both still run that binary, so nothing about it changes.

# Plan — an explicit DB context, and an answer that says which one

Two halves of one omission: the context can be GUESSED, and the answer never
says which one it used. Half 1 removes the guess; half 2 states the answer.

## 1. endless-go stops guessing

`monitor.SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox()` and its unconditional call in
`cmd/endless-go/main.go`'s startup path are DELETED, not gated. With no caller
left, `setDetectedContextDir` goes with it, and `dbContextFromFlag` collapses
into `dbContextDir != ""` — every context is a flag's now, so the
two-variable split that existed to tell a flag from a guess has nothing left to
tell apart.

`guardWorktreeDBContext` is unchanged. It already refuses when no explicit
context exists inside a self-dev worktree, and it already sits at the single
`DB()` entry point, so it covers every binary that opens the database
including future ones. It stopped firing because detection satisfied it; with
detection gone it fires again. Nothing about the gate was wrong.

`worktreeDBContextRefusal`'s wording changes: it currently says 'Invoke
through the endless CLI with --db main|sandbox, which threads --config-dir to
this binary', which stops being true once endless-go takes --db itself.

## 2. What `--db` means on endless-go

`--db main|sandbox`, consumed before any subcommand body, replacing
`ConsumeDBContextFlag`'s `--config-dir`.

  - `main` → the main config dir.
  - `sandbox` → this worktree's sandbox dir, refused when cwd is not inside a
    self-dev worktree, exactly as Python's `apply_db_choice` already refuses it.

The subtle part, stated so it is not re-litigated later: `--db sandbox` still
reads cwd, because cwd is what says WHICH worktree's sandbox. That is not the
guess coming back. The flag grants permission to open a database; cwd supplies
the address of the one permitted. What is being removed is cwd granting the
permission.

Subcommands that open no database — `task-status`, `session-state`,
`markdown`, `template` — do not accept `--db`; an unknown flag there is a
usage error, as today.

## 3. `--config-dir` retires

Every current caller moves to `--db`, and the ones that genuinely target a
throwaway directory move to `--db-dir <path>`, which keeps an escape without
keeping a second spelling of the normal case.

Note while auditing: `main_config_dir()` is `Path.home()/.config/endless`, so
it FOLLOWS $HOME even though it deliberately ignores $XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Any
caller that already runs under a temp HOME — the verify runner does — is
therefore served by plain `--db main` and needs no escape at all. Decide
per call site rather than converting them all to `--db-dir` by reflex; the
escape is for callers that must name a directory WITHOUT owning the process
environment, chiefly Go tests using `t.TempDir()`.

## 4. Every read AND WRITE states what answered it

One rule, so the three cases below are a rule and not a list:
ANNOUNCE WHAT THE INVOCATION RESOLVED, WHEN IT COULD HAVE RESOLVED OTHERWISE.

  - The DATABASE, in a self-dev project: ALWAYS. Either database could have
    been right on any invocation, so there is no case where the answer was
    never in doubt.
  - The PROJECT, downstream (non-self-dev): ONLY when the resolved project is
    not the one enclosing cwd — a `--project` flag, a session binding, or a
    cwd outside any registered project. With one database and usually one
    project, always-on is repetition, and repetition where nothing varies is
    how a line stops being read.
  - PINNED-IN-CODE contexts: NEVER. See §5 — a pin is not a resolution.

Surfaces:

  - MACHINE formats (`--json`, `--tsv`): a field in the payload. Per-row for
    array payloads (non-breaking — `list-live`'s rows already carry
    `project_id`), once at top level for object payloads.
  - The AGENT-FACING output mode and HUMAN output: in-band on stdout. Where a
    header already names the project — `session list`'s
    `Sessions — project: probe` — the database joins it there rather than
    taking a line of its own. (That mode's flag is `--llm` at the time of
    writing and is being renamed to `--agent` by a concurrent task; this plan
    depends on the mode, not on its spelling. Use whichever name is in the tree
    when this is implemented.)
  - WRITES announce as well as reads. E-1429's founding incident was a WRITE —
    a test `endless task add` that landed in the real ledger as E-1425 — and a
    write to the wrong database is the damaging case, where a wrong read only
    misleads. A mutating command names the database alongside what it changed.

NOT on stderr, deliberately, departing from `rowcap.echo_footer`: that footer
is prose COMMENTARY ABOUT an answer and would corrupt a payload, whereas the
store a result came from is DATA ABOUT THE RESULT and belongs in it. The
analysis records why stderr loses against an agent specifically.

## 5. The exemption

Contexts PINNED IN CODE announce nothing: the hook (`ForceRealDB`), and
`tmux`, `session-status` and `project-status` (`PinMainDB`). If the caller
could not have influenced the choice there is nothing to disambiguate, and the
tmux status line has no room for it. This is §4's rule, not an exception to it.

## 6. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-1668/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit: `internal/monitor` (the gate and its truth table),
   `internal/sessionquerycmd`, and the Python suite.
2. THE INCIDENT, as a regression test. From inside a worktree, using main's
   binary: `endless-go session-query list-live --project-root <main>` with no
   `--db` must REFUSE, naming the remedy. The same call with `--db main` must
   return main's rows. That single pair is the whole of half 1 — it is the
   exact command that silently answered from the sandbox.
3. `SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox` is absent from the tree; no call site remains.
4. No `--config-dir` survives outside the `--db-dir` escape.
5. Provenance, reads: a `--json` read carries the database and project; the
   same read under `--db main` and `--db sandbox` reports different values,
   from a seeded throwaway pair so the difference is checkable rather than
   asserted.
6. Provenance, writes: a `task add` against a seeded sandbox names the
   sandbox in its confirmation. This is E-1425's incident, inverted into a test.
7. The downstream rule: with a single non-self-dev project, a read from inside
   its checkout prints NO project line, and the same read with `--project`
   naming another does.
8. The exemption holds: the tmux status line's bytes are unchanged.

## 7. Not in scope

  - Python's `--db` requirement. It already refuses without the flag inside a
    self-dev worktree; this task changes nothing there.
  - E-1429's gate design. It was right; it was defeated.
  - Renaming the agent-facing output flag. A concurrent task owns `--llm` →
    `--agent`; this one consumes whatever it lands.
## 8. Decided during implementation

Three departures from §4 as written, recorded here so a reviewer meets them in
the plan rather than discovering them in the diff.

**`--tsv` carries nothing.** §4 said machine formats carry a field, naming
`--json` and `--tsv`. `endless sql` is the only `--tsv` surface, its rows are
the columns of arbitrary SQL, and it emits no header row — so the only thing a
"field" could mean there is a trailing column on every row, which silently
changes what every `cut -fN` and `while read` consumer sees. §4's own
justification for putting the trace in the payload was that doing so is
NON-breaking; for TSV it is not. Owner's call, 2026-09-16.

**The in-band line is one trailing line from one choke point, not folded into
each command's header.** §4 illustrated the rule with `session list`'s
`Sessions — project: probe`, the database joining it there. The trace is instead
written by the root group's result callback, so every command has it and a new
one cannot omit it. Where §4's both-ends intent does apply — the agent-facing
renders — a matching leading copy is emitted at the top of each, byte-identical
to the trailing one, on E-2097's rule.

**The Go layer announces the DATABASE only; the PROJECT half lives in Python.**
§4's project bullet fires downstream, and downstream `endless-go` is Python's
helper rather than anything a user types. Threading a resolved project name
through every internal verb would have put the fact where nobody reads it.

### Known limitation, from §4's own shape rule

An ARRAY payload carries the field per row, so a `--json` render of ZERO rows
carries no provenance at all — and "no rows" is exactly the shape the founding
incident took. The alternative is an envelope, which is the breaking change
per-row injection was chosen to avoid. Left as-is; an object payload and every
non-empty array are covered, as is the in-band line on the human and agent
surfaces.

# Plan — the flag surface, and the three choices it turned on

Scope is the flag surface, as the description fixes it. No new renderings.

## The surface, counted

`--llm` sits on **15** commands, not the 12 the description names — `task
landed` and `task unlanded` arrived later via E-2095 and take the pair from
the `landing_report_options` factory, which is why a source count of
`@click.option("--llm"` misses them.

- **13 carry `--llm` and `--json`**: `task list`, `task show` (and its
  `detail` alias), `task next`, `task active`, `task recent`, `task landed`,
  `task unlanded`, `task unsettled`, `task search`, `decision list`,
  `decision show`, `epic list`, `epic show`.
- **2 carry `--llm` alone** and gain `--json` here: `task deps`,
  `task relations`.
- **15 carry `--json` alone**: `project status`, `session show`,
  `session history`, `session status`, `session list`, `session search`,
  `session order`, `task next revise`, `worktree list`, `worktree current`,
  `worktree show`, `worktree for-task`, `worktree diagnose`, `verb list`,
  `phrase list`. The description's 16th is `task import --json`, which names
  an INPUT file rather than an output rendering and is therefore not part of
  this surface at all.

## Three choices the description left open (Mike, 2026-09-16)

**1. `--format` reaches every command with an output flag.** Not only the
agent-facing ones. A command with an agent rendering takes
`--format text|json|agent`; a command without one takes `--format text|json`.
One spelling that works everywhere beats a spelling that works on half the
surface and leaves an agent to learn which half.

**2. A command with no agent rendering does not ADVERTISE `agent`, but still
RECOGNISES it.** Its `--help` metavar reads `[text|json]`, so nothing learns a
value that command cannot honour. Passing `--format agent` there is still
parsed and refused by name, with `--format json` named first as the remedy per
ED-1584 — an agent that guesses gets a pointer, not Click's generic "is not one
of", and never a rendering it cannot read. This needs a custom `ParamType`
rather than `click.Choice`, which cannot separate what it advertises from what
it accepts.

**3. `session status` gets the flag and not the rendering.** E-1504's analysis
argues this sweep must give `session status` an agent view carrying the
ownership signal (`relation`, `in_flight`) in words where the human view prints
`●`/`⟳`. The description, written later, rules agent renderings for the
`--json`-only commands out of scope, and it governs — that work is also
two-language, since `session status` is Go (`internal/sessionstatuscmd`). The
analysis moves to E-2141 so the requirement outlives this task rather than
landing with it.

## How the rename is done

`--llm` is **retired, not aliased** — `retired_option("--llm", "--agent")`, the
pattern E-1000 established for `--text` → `--plan`. The flag stays declared and
hidden, so it never works and never degrades to "No such option": an agent
reaching for muscle memory is told where the flag went. That is the removal the
description asks for; a *working* alias is what no-legacy forbids, and this is
not one.

The internal `llm=` keyword renames to `agent=` alongside it, across
`task_cmd`, `decision_cmd`, `epic_cmd`, `session_cmd` and `rowcap`. A rename
that stops at the CLI leaves the codebase carrying the name it just retired.

## Contradiction is refused, not resolved

`--json`, `--agent` and `--format <fmt>` are three spellings of one setting.
Naming two DIFFERENT renderings (`--json --agent`, `--agent --format json`) is
a `UsageError` naming both spellings. Naming the same one twice is fine.

This is a deliberate behaviour change: today `--llm --json` silently yields
JSON, because every renderer tests `as_json` before `llm`. Silently picking a
winner is the silent incorrectness E-2143 exists to end — a wrong guess must
cost tokens.

## New module

`src/endless/outfmt.py` holds the whole surface: the `ParamType`, the
`output_options(*, agent=...)` decorator factory that declares
`--agent`/`--llm`-retired/`--json`/`--format` from the single fact of whether
the command has an agent rendering, and the resolution that collapses the three
into the `agent` / `as_json` keywords the renderers already take. One module so
a command declares what renderings it HAS and gets its flags from that, rather
than 30 hand-maintained copies drifting apart.

## Docs

`docs/guide/tasks.md`, `decisions.md`, `index.md` and `reference.md` name
`--llm` in 11 places; all move to `--agent`, and the guide gains `--format`.
`just guide-check` gates this.

## Out of scope, explicitly

Agent renderings for the 15 `--json`-only commands (E-2136 detail-shaped,
E-2141 list-shaped). Landed verify suites under `.endless/tasks/` that assert
`--llm` strings are left alone per `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.

already take BEFORE the command body runs, so it costs the renderers nothing
and is an alias rather than a third thing to branch on.

The renamed internals reach further than the CLI: the `llm=` keyword is now
`agent=` across `task_cmd`, `decision_cmd`, `epic_cmd`, `session_cmd` and
`rowcap`, and in the test suite's own fixture names.

## Docs

`docs/guide/tasks.md`, `decisions.md`, `index.md` and `reference.md` name
`--llm` in 11 places; all move to `--agent`, and the guide gains `--format`.
`just guide-check` gates this.

## Out of scope, explicitly

Agent renderings for the 15 `--json`-only commands (E-2136 detail-shaped,
E-2141 list-shaped). Landed verify suites under `.endless/tasks/` that assert
`--llm` strings are left alone per `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.

## Durable coverage

`tests/test_output_format.py` (18 tests), including a **drift guard** that walks
the whole command tree: `--json` without `--format` fails, `--format` without
`--json` fails, `--format` advertises `agent` iff the command has `--agent`, and
every `--agent` command still carries a hidden `--llm` pointer. The two
input-`--json` commands are an explicit named exception, so a third one is a
deliberate act with a test to change rather than a silent omission.

This is the guard the surface lacked: `--llm` reached 15 of 30 commands and
`--json` 28 precisely because nothing asserted they travel together.

# Plan — an explicit DB context, and an answer that says which one

Two halves of one omission: the context can be GUESSED, and the answer never
says which one it used. Half 1 removes the guess; half 2 states the answer.

## 1. endless-go stops guessing

`monitor.SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox()` and its unconditional call in
`cmd/endless-go/main.go`'s startup path are DELETED, not gated. With no caller
left, `setDetectedContextDir` goes with it, and `dbContextFromFlag` collapses
into `dbContextDir != ""` — every context is a flag's now, so the
two-variable split that existed to tell a flag from a guess has nothing left to
tell apart.

`guardWorktreeDBContext` is unchanged. It already refuses when no explicit
context exists inside a self-dev worktree, and it already sits at the single
`DB()` entry point, so it covers every binary that opens the database
including future ones. It stopped firing because detection satisfied it; with
detection gone it fires again. Nothing about the gate was wrong.

`worktreeDBContextRefusal`'s wording changes: it currently says 'Invoke
through the endless CLI with --db main|sandbox, which threads --config-dir to
this binary', which stops being true once endless-go takes --db itself.

## 2. What `--db` means on endless-go

`--db main|sandbox`, consumed before any subcommand body, replacing
`ConsumeDBContextFlag`'s `--config-dir`.

  - `main` → the main config dir.
  - `sandbox` → this worktree's sandbox dir, refused when cwd is not inside a
    self-dev worktree, exactly as Python's `apply_db_choice` already refuses it.

The subtle part, stated so it is not re-litigated later: `--db sandbox` still
reads cwd, because cwd is what says WHICH worktree's sandbox. That is not the
guess coming back. The flag grants permission to open a database; cwd supplies
the address of the one permitted. What is being removed is cwd granting the
permission.

Subcommands that open no database — `task-status`, `session-state`,
`markdown`, `template` — do not accept `--db`; an unknown flag there is a
usage error, as today.

## 3. `--config-dir` retires

Every current caller moves to `--db`, and the ones that genuinely target a
throwaway directory move to `--db-dir <path>`, which keeps an escape without
keeping a second spelling of the normal case.

Note while auditing: `main_config_dir()` is `Path.home()/.config/endless`, so
it FOLLOWS $HOME even though it deliberately ignores $XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Any
caller that already runs under a temp HOME — the verify runner does — is
therefore served by plain `--db main` and needs no escape at all. Decide
per call site rather than converting them all to `--db-dir` by reflex; the
escape is for callers that must name a directory WITHOUT owning the process
environment, chiefly Go tests using `t.TempDir()`.

## 4. Every read AND WRITE states what answered it

One rule, so the three cases below are a rule and not a list:
ANNOUNCE WHAT THE INVOCATION RESOLVED, WHEN IT COULD HAVE RESOLVED OTHERWISE.

  - The DATABASE, in a self-dev project: ALWAYS. Either database could have
    been right on any invocation, so there is no case where the answer was
    never in doubt.
  - The PROJECT, downstream (non-self-dev): ONLY when the resolved project is
    not the one enclosing cwd — a `--project` flag, a session binding, or a
    cwd outside any registered project. With one database and usually one
    project, always-on is repetition, and repetition where nothing varies is
    how a line stops being read.
  - PINNED-IN-CODE contexts: NEVER. See §5 — a pin is not a resolution.

Surfaces:

  - MACHINE formats (`--json`, `--tsv`): a field in the payload. Per-row for
    array payloads (non-breaking — `list-live`'s rows already carry
    `project_id`), once at top level for object payloads.
  - The AGENT-FACING output mode and HUMAN output: in-band on stdout. Where a
    header already names the project — `session list`'s
    `Sessions — project: probe` — the database joins it there rather than
    taking a line of its own. (That mode's flag is `--llm` at the time of
    writing and is being renamed to `--agent` by a concurrent task; this plan
    depends on the mode, not on its spelling. Use whichever name is in the tree
    when this is implemented.)
  - WRITES announce as well as reads. E-1429's founding incident was a WRITE —
    a test `endless task add` that landed in the real ledger as E-1425 — and a
    write to the wrong database is the damaging case, where a wrong read only
    misleads. A mutating command names the database alongside what it changed.

NOT on stderr, deliberately, departing from `rowcap.echo_footer`: that footer
is prose COMMENTARY ABOUT an answer and would corrupt a payload, whereas the
store a result came from is DATA ABOUT THE RESULT and belongs in it. The
analysis records why stderr loses against an agent specifically.

## 5. The exemption

Contexts PINNED IN CODE announce nothing: the hook (`ForceRealDB`), and
`tmux`, `session-status` and `project-status` (`PinMainDB`). If the caller
could not have influenced the choice there is nothing to disambiguate, and the
tmux status line has no room for it. This is §4's rule, not an exception to it.

## 6. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-1668/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit: `internal/monitor` (the gate and its truth table),
   `internal/sessionquerycmd`, and the Python suite.
2. THE INCIDENT, as a regression test. From inside a worktree, using main's
   binary: `endless-go session-query list-live --project-root <main>` with no
   `--db` must REFUSE, naming the remedy. The same call with `--db main` must
   return main's rows. That single pair is the whole of half 1 — it is the
   exact command that silently answered from the sandbox.
3. `SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox` is absent from the tree; no call site remains.
4. No `--config-dir` survives outside the `--db-dir` escape.
5. Provenance, reads: a `--json` read carries the database and project; the
   same read under `--db main` and `--db sandbox` reports different values,
   from a seeded throwaway pair so the difference is checkable rather than
   asserted.
6. Provenance, writes: a `task add` against a seeded sandbox names the
   sandbox in its confirmation. This is E-1425's incident, inverted into a test.
7. The downstream rule: with a single non-self-dev project, a read from inside
   its checkout prints NO project line, and the same read with `--project`
   naming another does.
8. The exemption holds: the tmux status line's bytes are unchanged.

## 7. Not in scope

  - Python's `--db` requirement. It already refuses without the flag inside a
    self-dev worktree; this task changes nothing there.
  - E-1429's gate design. It was right; it was defeated.
  - Renaming the agent-facing output flag. A concurrent task owns `--llm` →
    `--agent`; this one consumes whatever it lands.
## 8. Decided during implementation

Three departures from §4 as written, recorded here so a reviewer meets them in
the plan rather than discovering them in the diff.

**`--tsv` carries nothing.** §4 said machine formats carry a field, naming
`--json` and `--tsv`. `endless sql` is the only `--tsv` surface, its rows are
the columns of arbitrary SQL, and it emits no header row — so the only thing a
"field" could mean there is a trailing column on every row, which silently
changes what every `cut -fN` and `while read` consumer sees. Owner's call,
2026-09-16.

**An array payload is WRAPPED, not tagged per row.** §4 said per-row, on the
grounds that a new envelope "is a breaking change to every consumer". Measured,
that was 4 Python call sites, 11 test assertions and no external consumer — all
in this repo and updatable in the same change. Per-row was wrong on three
counts besides: it said nothing at all for an EMPTY result, which is precisely
the shape the founding incident took; it repeated one identical object once per
row; and it left Endless with two JSON shapes for one question when
`session-status` and `project-status` had been returning `{…, "rows": [...]}`
all along. The wrap is unconditional, so the shape never varies. Owner's call,
2026-09-16.

**The in-band line is one trailing line from one shared function, not folded
into each command's header.** §4 illustrated the rule with `session list`'s
`Sessions — project: probe`, the database joining it there. The trace is instead
written by the root group's result callback, so every command has it and a new
one cannot omit it. Where §4's both-ends intent applies — the agent-facing
renders — a matching leading copy is emitted at the top of each, byte-identical
to the trailing one, on E-2097's rule.

**The Go layer announces the DATABASE only; the PROJECT half lives in Python.**
§4's project bullet fires downstream, and downstream `endless-go` is Python's
helper rather than anything a user types. Threading a resolved project name
through every internal verb would have put the fact where nobody reads it.

### Two flaws this work exposed rather than caused

`sessionquerycmd.TestTaskReport_BinaryEmitsFacts` asserted "the child E-12 is
off the wire" as `strings.Contains(out, "12")` over the whole payload. Any "12"
anywhere satisfied it — a timestamp, a row count — and once the payload carried
a `t.TempDir()` path, whose random digits contain "12" about one run in ten, the
test became intermittently red. Now asserted against the decoded task-fact keys.

The machine-format suppression read `sys.argv`. `click.testing.CliRunner` passes
its arguments to `Command.main` directly and leaves `sys.argv` as pytest's, so
the scan was right in production and silently wrong under test — surfacing only
as test-order-dependent noise. It now takes argv as an argument, from
`DBAwareGroup.main`, which already pre-scans it for `--db`.

# E-2083 — as implemented

## Restore the four E-2074 deleted

`.endless/tasks/e-{1568,1570,1572,1621}/verify.sh`, content taken from
`bf285b54^:tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh`.

The three project-wide sweeps that crossed every suite after E-2074 are applied
to them, because they were already deleted when those sweeps ran and restoring
a file means putting it where it would be now:

- E-2023 (`c79857dfc`, `d3cf23423`) — relocation to `.endless/tasks/<id>/`,
  the harness-source block as the first executable statement, the header
  run-line rewritten to `endless task verify E-NNNN`, prose path references
  rewritten.
- E-2090 (`53376963c`, `971636d16`) — the four-line DO-NOT-EDIT banner below
  the shebang (via the idempotent `just suite-banner`), and the executable bit.

Without them `tests/test_suite_guard.py` fails: it parametrizes over every
suite and requires banner, harness-first-line and the x bit.

## Revert the ten it amended

`e-{1573,1624,1645,1648,1659,1905,1906,1914,1967,2067}`. Nine reverse-applied
cleanly from E-2074's own diff. e-1573's first hunk was done by hand because
E-2023 had since rewritten the run-line inside it.

The task title says eight; the commit amended ten, as the analysis field lists.
Ten are reverted.

### The per-file judgment the task asked for

E-2074's message defends three amendments as fixes to real pre-existing
leftovers. All three claims are false — each thing was live in the tree at
`bf285b54^`, the commit's own parent, and was made stale BY E-2074 in the same
commit that then "fixed" the suite for it:

| claim | state at `bf285b54^` |
|---|---|
| e-1573 asserted the guide documents `bg_throttle_warn` | live in `src/endless/task_cmd.py` AND in `docs/guide/orchestration.md` |
| e-1914 probed `sessions.summary` | declared in `internal/schema/schema.sql` |
| e-2067 probed `session.go` for `nearestEpicAncestor` | present in `internal/monitor/session.go` |

So all ten are retrofits and revert uniformly. Section 5 of the suite asserts
this against git history rather than leaving it as prose.

## E-2074's own suite: deliberately untouched

The task description's last step assumed its four `assert_absent` lines would
start failing. They do not: they name the pre-E-2023 paths
(`tests/tasks/e-1568-verify.sh`), which stay gone, and its reference sweep
greps only `cmd internal src tests docs justfile`, never `.endless/`. Nothing
in it breaks, so editing it would commit this task's own sin while reverting
it. Mike's call, this session. Section 6 asserts it was left alone.

## GROWN SCOPE — the harness TAP defect

Found while mutation-testing this task's own suite; folded in on Mike's call
(ED-1550: fold a finding into an open task rather than file).

`_harness.sh`'s `tap()` wrote its argument to the runner's TAP stream with
`printf '%s\n' "$1"`, so a multi-line `actual` — a diff, or `tail -25` of a log
— put unprefixed lines mid-stream. The runner's parser stopped counting where
it met one: a run that was really 1 failed / 53 passed was reported as
1 failed / 18 passed, with the suite's own on-screen summary still correct. It
under-reported only on a FAILING run, which is exactly when the count is read.
30 landed suites pass a multi-line `actual` today.

- `tap()` now emits every line after the first as a `# ` diagnostic, which TAP
  attaches to the record it follows. Single-line calls are byte-identical.
- `tests/test_suite_guard.py` gains two durable tests: one proving a multi-line
  detail stays one densely-numbered record with its detail intact (it fails
  against the old `tap()`), one pinning that single-line records are unchanged.
  The coverage lives there, not only here, because a fix protected solely by a
  land-time suite is unprotected the moment this task lands.

Blast radius is asserted, not assumed: section 6 confirms the only files
touched outside the fifteen suites are `_harness.sh` and its test, that the
harness still defines exactly the same functions by name, and that every
non-comment line the edit changed is inside `tap()`.

## Verify

gate (`tests/test_suite_guard.py`, `tests/test_suite_rules.py`). Section 3 is
