payload.title: An output flag advertises only the renderings a command actually has, and refuses the rest by name rather than falling back
payload.description: Where a command has no agent rendering, --format agent is refused by name with the rendering that works named first (ED-1584), rather than advertising a value the command cannot honour or quietly returning the human view. Rejected: silent fallback, which would hand an agent session status's glyph-encoded ownership signal as if it were agent-facing, the failure E-2143 exists to end; and advertising the full set everywhere, honest at the call and dishonest in --help. click.Choice cannot separate the advertised set from the accepted set, so a custom parameter type is the cost of the rule. Generalizes beyond output formats: when a capability arrives surface by surface, a place that lacks it refuses by name and says what to use instead. Decided by Mike during E-1504; binds E-2136 and E-2141 as agent renderings arrive command by command.

fields.analysis:
Also removes E-1818's schema-passive mode, which becomes unnecessary once no connect applies schema: the mode exists to stop a binary mutating a DB it merely opened, and nothing needs suppressing when nothing applies.

## Measured during E-2019 — the real ledger does not match its own version

E-2019 records the ledger at schema version 1. That version is the shape schema.sql produced, and the ledger is NOT that shape. Measured 2026-09-16 against a VACUUM INTO snapshot (127MB, 1,448 tasks, 1,199 sessions), compared with a database freshly built from schema.sql:

- Columns schema.sql declares that the ledger lacks: NONE. It is a superset, never a subset.
- Extra column: tasks.focus_id, left by the deleted focuses feature.
- DEFAULT drift: tasks.status defaults to 'needs_plan' — the pre-rename status name, which is no longer a valid status. Any INSERT omitting status writes an invalid value.
- Trigger body drift: tasks_updated_at lacks the `AND updated_at != strftime(...)` guard schema.sql declares.
- Column ORDER differs on 4 tables (tasks, errors, decisions, task_landings) — ALTER-appended rather than declared order.
- 11 leftover tables, 7 indexes and 1 trigger from removed features are still present: channels, conversations, messages, session_navigations, nav_via_kinds, focuses, suggestions, task_files, project_next_items, project_next_revisions, session_kinds. Several are marked APPLIED in _schema_version by change files whose DROP never took effect (e-2029-drop-channel-tables and e-2081-drop-session-navigations are both recorded applied while their tables survive).

Consequence for this task: "the database agrees with the binary" cannot be implemented as a shape comparison. Version equality is the only check the real ledger can pass. If E-2020 ever wants a stronger check than the recorded integer, it needs a reconciliation migration first — that is a separate piece of work, not a tightening of the gate.

## What E-2019 leaves for this task to build on

- schema.Migrate(db) is the single way a database acquires its schema (monitor.DB, the sandbox seeder, the ledger projector, tests).
- schema.DBVersion(ctx, db) reads the version a database is recorded at; schema.LatestVersion() reads the highest version the BINARY carries. E-2020's direction rules are a comparison of those two.
- schema.Seed(db) applies the enum mirrors and is called on every Migrate. It is deliberately NOT a migration: it preserves E-1659's self-heal. When E-2020 stops applying schema on connect, decide explicitly whether Seed keeps running — the enum gates in monitor.DB() depend on it.
- 00001_baseline.sql is the only migration allowed to be idempotent (every statement carries IF NOT EXISTS). A later migration must not copy that.

## What E-2019 leaves this task to generate from

The migration set is internal/schema/migrations/, embedded via //go:embed and driven by goose as a library. 00001_baseline.sql was produced by dumping sqlite_master, in creation order, from a database built by schema.sql, then mechanically re-injecting IF NOT EXISTS (SQLite does not store that clause, and the baseline must stay idempotent so the real ledger reaches version 1 by an inert replay). The generator used is a throwaway; this task writes the durable one, in the other direction.

Three things a naive generator would get wrong:

1. FTS5 shadow tables. schema.sql declares one virtual table, session_messages_fts. SQLite then creates session_messages_fts_data/_idx/_docsize/_config, and those appear in sqlite_master like any other table. Declaring them is wrong — the fts5 module owns them. Detect with `SELECT name FROM pragma_table_list WHERE type='shadow'` (SQLite 3.37+), not by name pattern.
2. The enum seeds are NOT in the migration set. They live in internal/schema/seeds.sql and are applied by schema.Seed() after every migration run, so E-1659's self-heal survives. A generated schema.sql that omits them describes a database that fails every integrity gate on first connect; a generated one that includes them has to say where they actually come from.
3. The three leading PRAGMAs (journal_mode, busy_timeout, foreign_keys) are not in the migration set either — they configure a connection, and journal_mode cannot change inside goose's transaction. Every opener sets them itself.

## The cost this task should weigh explicitly

schema.sql is 1,323 lines, and a large fraction of it is commentary that exists nowhere else — the E-1960 index-naming trap, the E-1929 view-vs-index ordering constraint, the ID-append rule on session_task_relations, the reasoning behind the write-once trigger. A generator that emits DDL produces a file that is accurate and says none of that. The description's fallback ("delete schema.sql rather than keep a hand-maintained copy") would delete the commentary with it. Consider a third option: move the prose into the migrations that own each object, so generation has something to carry forward.

While both files exist, internal/schema/migrate_test.go's TestMigrate_MatchesSchemaSQL pins them equal in both directions — a schema.sql edited without a migration fails, and a migration added without mirroring into schema.sql fails. That test is what this task replaces with real generation.

## sqlc, if it is still on the roadmap

Checked 2026-09-16. sqlc reads a goose migration directory natively (schema: <migrations dir>, engine: "sqlite"; sqlc names atlas, dbmate, golang-migrate, goose, sql-migrate and tern) and ignores Down sections. Two constraints worth keeping in mind here, because they shape what the migration set may contain:

- sqlc parses migration files in LEXICOGRAPHIC order, which diverges from goose's numeric order unless filenames are zero-padded. 00001_baseline.sql already is; keep the padding.
- sqlc can only read SQL migrations. A goose GO migration is invisible to it, so any DDL expressed in Go silently disappears from the schema sqlc models. Keep DDL in .sql migrations and put data work in a separate step.
- sqlc gained virtual-table/FTS5 support in 1.31.0 with known rough edges (the fts5 token is case-sensitive — this schema spells it lowercase, which is the working case — and the implicit rowid is not modeled). session_messages_fts is the one object most likely to need attention if sqlc is adopted.

payload.title: Give cmd/endless-migrate the same --db vocabulary as endless-go
payload.description: endless-go takes --db main|sandbox with --db-dir as the escape; cmd/endless-migrate still takes --config-dir, the flag E-1668 retired from the other binary. One product, one concept, two vocabularies — and the split already forced a fork in the Python layer that nearly shipped a broken land.
payload.analysis:
Endless has two Go binaries that both need to be told which database to open, and since E-1668 they take different words for it. `endless-go` takes `--db main|sandbox`, with `--db-dir ` as the escape. `cmd/endless-migrate` (ED-1571) takes `--config-dir ` — the flag E-1668 retired from the other binary. One product, one concept, two vocabularies. ## Why it matters The guide teaches `--db`. A reader who learns it and then reaches for the migration executable is wrong, and nothing tells them so at the point of use. It also costs a fork in the Python layer: `config.go_db_context_args()` and `config.migrate_db_context_args()` exist solely because the two binaries disagree, and every future caller has to know which one it is talking to. That fork already produced a near-miss. `worktree land` shells to endless-migrate and threaded `go_db_context_args()`; when E-1668 changed that to emit `--db main`, endless-migrate could not parse it — `--db` survives its strip, lands in `argv[1]` where the subcommand belongs, and the migration fails mid-land. The binary's own test stubbed the helper, so the suite stayed green while every real land would have broken. One vocabulary removes the class of mistake, not just the instance. ## The design question this carries `--db sandbox` resolves from cwd. `internal/dbcontext` is deliberately cwd-free — ED-1571's whole claim is that a tool which rewrites a schema resolves its target from what the caller NAMED, never from where it happens to be standing. So the two binaries cannot take an identical flag set, and the proposal is: - `endless-migrate --db main` → the main database ($HOME-following, no cwd) - `endless-migrate --db-dir

` → name a directory outright (today's `--config-dir`, renamed) - `endless-migrate --db sandbox` → REFUSED, naming why: this executable has no cwd routing, so there is no "which sandbox" for it to answer. That is the same vocabulary minus the one value that would contradict ED-1571, rather than a second dialect. Whether the refusal is the right call, or whether `--db` should simply not appear on this binary at all and only `--db-dir` should, is the thing to settle in the plan. ## Scope - `internal/dbcontext`: `ConfigDirFlag` and `ConsumeConfigDirFlag` gain the new spelling. The package is shared, so its parser is the single place. - `cmd/endless-migrate/main.go`: usage text, package doc, and the "Neither --config-dir nor XDG_CONFIG_HOME nor a home directory" error. - `src/endless/config.py`: whether the two helpers merge back into one is part of the design — they can, if endless-migrate accepts everything `go_db_context_args` can emit except `--db sandbox`, and the land always pins main. - Tests: `internal/dbcontext/dbcontext_test.go`, `internal/schemachange/executable_test.go` (3 sites), `tests/test_worktree_land_migrate_exec.py`, and the doc comment on `runner.DefaultDBPath` in `internal/schema/changes/runner`, which names the flag in prose (`grep -rn -- --config-dir internal/schema` finds it). ## The transition hazard, which this task should not repeat E-1668's own land failed once on exactly this: the `just land` Python process had imported main's PRE-merge source, advanced main, then emitted the landing event with the old spelling to a binary built from the new one. Version skew across a process boundary, for one invocation, in the window the land itself opens. The ff-merge was idempotent and a re-run recorded it, but the failure is inherent to changing a cross-process flag contract in a self_dev land. Decide in the plan how to avoid it: accept both spellings for one landing and remove the old one in a follow-up, or establish that the land's own event write must not straddle the merge. ## Not in scope - Which executable performs a land-time migration. ED-1571 stands. - endless-go's flags. E-1668 settled those.

triage.rationale: The target vocabulary (--db main|sandbox with --db-dir as escape) is already defined by endless-go's precedent, so the change is a mechanical alignment of endless-migrate's flags to that existing contract.

payload.title: Delete the change-file mechanism and move land-time apply onto goose
payload.description: E-2019's Increment 4, split out because it reworks the land path and cmd/endless-migrate, which landed the same day. E-2019 made goose the source of the schema but deleted nothing, so both mechanisms are now live side by side; this removes the old one. Covers internal/schema/changes/ and its runner, the _schema_version table, the apply-change surface in Go and Python, db.py's dead legacy migrator, and reworking worktree land's apply step from per-change-file to a goose 'up'.
payload.analysis:
## Scope

Delete the per-ticket change-file mechanism now that goose owns the schema:

- internal/schema/changes/ -- 38 files (15 .go, 23 .sql) plus the runner package, ~2,700 lines.
- The _schema_version table, its declaration in schema.sql, and therefore its statement in 00001_baseline.sql.
- `endless-go event apply-change`, `endless db apply-change`, event_bridge.apply_change.
- db.py's dead legacy migrator: _migrate, _migrate_v2/v3/v5/v6, _should_auto_migrate, the ENDLESS_AUTO_MIGRATE environment variable, and the _has_table/_has_column helpers that serve only them. Its own docstring says it was slated for removal in E-894 Phase 5, and internal/monitor/migrate.go -- the thing that was to replace it -- was deleted by E-1459. It short-circuits at PRAGMA user_version >= 6 and the real ledger is at 12, so it does nothing there. It is NOT inert elsewhere: _backup_db() runs BEFORE the short-circuit test, on every Python connect, for any database below 6.

## The one real design step

E-2088 landed 2026-09-16 (901e589) and built cmd/endless-migrate around change FILES: `endless-migrate apply <change-file>`, invoked once per changed file by `worktree land` at Step 5.5, with the file list computed at Step 4.6 and the executable built by `just migrate-bin` in between. Under goose there are no change files to enumerate.

So the executable's subcommand becomes `up`, and the land's question changes from "which change files does this branch add" to "does this branch carry a migration the database has not got" -- schema.LatestVersion() (what the binary carries) compared against the database's recorded version, rather than a directory walk. internal/schemachange is then either deleted outright or reduced to whatever `up` still needs; the `.go` change runner goes with the change files it served.

Do not lose what E-2088 established while reworking it: the build-then-apply ordering (build at 4.6 while base is still untouched, apply at 5.5 between the ff-merge and the record), a build failure aborting with nothing merged and nothing migrated, and an apply failure producing the post-merge message that says re-run rather than restore.

## What E-2019 already verified for this task

internal/schemachange/executable_test.go asserts `go list -deps ./cmd/endless-migrate` links only dbcontext + schemachange + the cmd -- the property that a migration tool carries no code expecting a schema. internal/schema imports nothing but stdlib and github.com/pressly/goose/v3, so it satisfies that property as-is and the allowlist simply gains it. No restructuring is needed to let endless-migrate carry the goose set.

## Constraint

schema.sql must survive this task. It is still the readable artifact, and E-2021 is what turns it into a generated one; deleting it here leaves it deleted and unreplaced. Deleting only its _schema_version declaration is correct and sufficient.

triage.rationale: The description names the exact files/tables to delete and the exact replacement mechanism (goose 'up' in worktree land's apply step), leaving no material design decision open.

fields.plan:
# Plan

Mechanism only. E-2019 changes HOW the schema is defined and applied; it does
not change WHEN. At the end of this task `monitor.DB()` still brings a database
up to date on connect — it just does it by replaying goose migrations instead of
exec'ing `schema.sql`. E-2020 changes the semantics.

That split is what makes E-2019 landable on its own: the only new artifact in a
migrated database is goose's version table, which every existing binary ignores.
No older binary breaks, so this land does not need E-1972 or E-2088.

## Increment 1 — goose, and one baseline migration

- Add `github.com/pressly/goose/v3`. It is used as a LIBRARY against an existing
  `*sql.DB`, never as a CLI. Confirm at implementation time that
  `goose.SetDialect("sqlite3")` drives a `modernc.org/sqlite` connection — the
  project has no cgo and must keep it that way.
- `internal/schema/migrations/00001_baseline.sql`, embedded with `//go:embed` +
  `goose.SetBaseFS`, so the set ships inside the binary with no file dependency.
- **The baseline is the CURRENT shape and nothing else.** Migrations are forward
  looking from this point. No file under `internal/schema/changes/` becomes a
  migration; that directory served land-time application and is not a schema
  history. This is the decision that makes the whole task tractable — see the
  note at the end of the plan for what it discards.
- Generate the baseline from the live schema rather than by hand-copying
  `schema.sql`: dump `sqlite_master` from a database built by the current
  `schema.sql`, so what goose replays is provably what the code produces today.
  `schema.sql`'s `INSERT OR IGNORE` enum seeds go into the baseline too — a
  schema without `task_types`, `gate_kinds`, `process_kinds` and `nav_via_kinds`
  rows fails the integrity gates on first connect.

## Increment 2 — every database creation path moves to goose

- `monitor.DB()`: replace `Exec(schema.SQL)` with goose's up-to-latest against
  the same connection. Same timing, same effect, different source. The
  E-1818 schema-passive guard stays exactly as it is — E-2020 removes it.
- `seedFromWorktree` in `internal/sandboxcmd/seed_worktree.go` does the same.
- `src/endless/db.py` `_init_schema` no longer reads `schema.sql`. Python does
  not gain a migration runner; it shells out to Go, matching how
  `apply-change`, `backup` and `restore` already work.

## Increment 3 — tests build from a hashed template

45 Go files and the Python suite currently `Exec(schema.SQL)` per test. Replaying
the migration set per test is the honest thing and also the slow thing.

- One helper builds a database at the latest version ONCE per run, writes it to
  a template file, and every test copies that file.
- The template's filename carries a hash of the embedded migration set, so a new
  migration produces a different name and the stale one is never reused. That is
  the whole staleness defence; without it a cached fixture silently runs old
  schema against new code.
- Go and Python get the same helper shape, keyed on the same hash, so neither
  suite can drift from the other.

## Increment 4 — delete what goose replaces

- **`db.py`'s migrator goes entirely**: `_migrate`, `_migrate_v2`, `_migrate_v3`,
  `_migrate_v5`, `_migrate_v6`, `_should_auto_migrate`, the `ENDLESS_AUTO_MIGRATE`
  environment variable, and the `_has_table`/`_has_column` helpers that serve
  only them. It has been dead for a while and says so: its docstring reads
  "Once Go's framework (internal/monitor/migrate.go, E-863) owns the schema, this
  function becomes a no-op. Slated for removal in E-894 Phase 5", and
  `internal/monitor/migrate.go` was deleted by E-1459. It short-circuits at
  `PRAGMA user_version >= 6`; the real database is at 12.

  It is not entirely inert, which is the other reason to remove it: 98 sandbox
  databases sit at `user_version 0` and 59 at `5`, so they DO enter the ladder,
  where the DDL steps no-op against a `schema.sql`-built database but
  `_backup_db()` runs first, on every Python connect.

- **`internal/schema/changes/` and the `_schema_version` table go**, along with
  `endless db apply-change`, `event_bridge.apply_change`, the runner package
  (`internal/schema/changes/runner`), and `worktree land`'s apply step. Land-time
  schema application becomes E-2088's migration executable; until E-2088 lands,
  a branch carrying a migration is applied by whatever E-2020 defines. Sequencing
  note: this increment must not land before E-2088 exists, or a self_dev land has
  no way to apply anything. If E-2088 is not ready, stop after Increment 3 — the
  earlier increments stand on their own.

- `schema.sql` itself stays put and keeps being committed. E-2021 turns it into a
  generated artifact; this task must not leave it deleted and unreplaced.

## Increment 5 — baseline the databases that exist

- **The one real database** (`~/.config/endless/endless.db`) is stamped at the
  baseline version without replaying it. It already has the shape.
- **The 158 sandbox databases** under `~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/` are deleted
  and rebuilt lazily. They are cache — the directory says so — and rebuilding
  makes fresh-database-by-replay the path every sandbox exercises, rather than a
  branch taken only by new installs. Baselining them instead would mean stamping
  "this database is at the baseline" onto 98 databases at `user_version 0` whose
  real shape is whatever `schema.sql` looked like when they were made, which may
  not be true.

  A rebuilt sandbox is built at the latest version, so a worktree whose branch
  predates that version will find its sandbox ahead of its own binary. That is
  correct and is the signal, not a bug to accommodate: the worktree rebases onto
  main before it can use its sandbox again. Nothing here builds a sandbox at an
  older version to spare it that.
- Backups under `~/.config/endless/backups/` are not touched. A backup is a
  restore source, and restoring an old one produces a database behind the
  binary — which is exactly the case E-2020's direction rules handle.

# Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-2019/`, run only through the runner — `just verify E-2019`
(which routes `--db sandbox`, so the gate exercises the CANDIDATE binary rather
than main's) or `endless task verify E-2019`. Never executed directly: `_guard.sh`
refuses a direct run, because a direct run carries your real `HOME`.

Shape: a `verify.toml` whose first `[[check]]` is a `gotest` runner over the
migration unit tests — the fail-fast half — plus a `verify.sh` for the
end-to-end assertions that need a built database. The script sources
`_harness.sh`, opens with the DO-NOT-EDIT header naming E-2019, uses `section` /
`assert_eq` / `assert_contains`, and calls `summary` last. Any fixture it ships
is read from `$ENDLESS_VERIFY_DIR`, never a typed path.

The runner supplies the isolation — a temp `HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` — so
nothing here passes `--config-dir` to keep writes off the real ledger.

A suite here is a land-time gate for one task at one moment and nothing re-runs
it afterward, so coverage that must outlive the land is mirrored into the
durable suites: assertions 1 and 2 below are the schema's own invariants and
belong in `internal/schema`'s Go tests as well as here.

1. A fresh database built by replaying migrations is schema-identical to one
   built by the current `schema.sql`: compare normalised `sqlite_master` dumps.
   This is the assertion that the baseline is honest, and it must run against a
   `schema.sql` copy pinned in the test, not the live file, so a later edit to
   `schema.sql` fails the test rather than silently redefining the baseline.
2. Enum seed rows survive the replay: `task_types`, `gate_kinds`,
   `process_kinds` and `nav_via_kinds` all pass their `VerifyIntegrity` gates on
   a freshly replayed database.
3. Stamping is not replaying: a database already carrying the current shape is
   stamped at the baseline and no DDL runs against it.
4. The template is hash-keyed: change the embedded migration set, and the test
   helper builds a new template rather than reusing the old one.
5. `db.py` no longer creates or alters any schema object — assert by opening a
   database with an intentionally missing column and confirming Python surfaces
   an error rather than repairing it.
6. `_schema_version`, `internal/schema/changes/` and `endless db apply-change`
   are gone, and nothing references them.
7. No cgo: `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./...` succeeds.

# End of plan

What follows explains a choice that would otherwise look like an omission.

## Prior change files are not converted, deliberately

The obvious reading of "convert internal/schema to versioned migrations" is that
the 34 files under `internal/schema/changes/` become 34 goose migrations, with
the 12 `.go` ones becoming goose Go migrations. That is what E-2019's
description says, and it is not what this plan does.

Those files were written to be applied once, at land, to one database. They are
not a schema history and cannot be replayed as one. Measured on the real
database: `_schema_version` holds 46 rows — 12 legacy `vNN-` names from the
pre-ED-1472 framework plus 34 change basenames — while disk holds 34 files, and
the two sets do not agree in either direction. `e-1542-session-gates` is on disk
and was never applied; `e-1653-migrate-status-data` is applied and its file no
longer exists. Several files also rebuild tables into shapes that later files
rebuild again, so replaying them in order reconstructs a sequence of historical
schemas nobody needs and gets to the same place `schema.sql` describes now.

Converting them would mean auditing 34 files to determine which were ever
applied where, then writing a baselining scheme that maps a SET of basenames
onto a LINEAR version — for a history whose only surviving consumer is the one
database that already has the end state.

So the baseline is the current shape, migrations run forward from here, and the
change files are deleted rather than translated. The cost is that a database
older than the baseline cannot be migrated forward by goose. There is no such
database: there is one real database and it is current.

# As implemented — where this diverged from the plan above

Decided with Mike during implementation, 2026-09-16. The plan above is left as
written; this section records what actually shipped and why each departure was
made.

## Scope

- **Increments 1–3 shipped.** Increment 4 split out to **E-2158** (`--cleans-up
  E-2019`). E-2088 landed mid-session (901e589), which lifted the plan's own
  sequencing gate — but it landed built around change FILES
  (`endless-migrate apply <file>`), so Increment 4 now also means reworking
  E-2088's executable and `worktree land`'s apply step onto goose. That is a
  land-path change coupled to a program that landed the same day; it gets its
  own review and its own revert radius. Both schema mechanisms are live side by
  side until E-2158 lands.
- **Increment 5 collapsed.** Only one database matters — the real ledger — so
  there is no population of pre-versioning databases to design for, and no
  sandbox deletion sweep.

## Baselining: an inert replay, not a stamp

The plan and description say populated databases are "BASELINED, not
replayed". What shipped achieves the same outcome by a different means:
`00001_baseline.sql` carries `IF NOT EXISTS` on every statement, so the real
ledger's first connect replays it as a no-op and comes out recorded at version
1. Nothing stamps; there is no detection heuristic.

SQLite does not store `IF NOT EXISTS` in `sqlite_master`, so the generated dump
came back without it and the generator re-injects it. No parser: across the
whole schema the dumped statements open in exactly six forms, so it is a
known-token rewrite that raises on a seventh. This migration alone may be
idempotent; a later one must not copy it.

Proven against a VACUUM INTO snapshot of the live ledger (127MB, 1,448 tasks,
1,199 sessions): shape identical, row counts identical, 40ms, version 1.

## Enum seeds are not in the baseline

They live in `internal/schema/seeds.sql` and `schema.Seed()` applies them after
every `Migrate`, preserving E-1659's self-heal (upserts that reconcile an enum
row renamed out from under the database). A migration runs once and would have
silently removed that behaviour.

## Test fixtures: mechanical swap, no template cache

72 call sites across 36 test files swap `db.Exec(schema.SQL)` for
`schema.Migrate(db)`. Measured: `Migrate` 4.5ms vs `Exec(schema.SQL)` 9.9ms —
goose runs the set in one transaction. The hash-keyed template cache optimises
a cost that is currently negative, and can be added later once every site
already funnels through `schema.Migrate`. `Migrate` works on `:memory:`, so no
test's storage changed.

## Things found along the way

- **Foreign keys.** `schema.sql`'s leading `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` enforced
  FKs as a side effect of being exec'd. Leaving the PRAGMAs out of the baseline
  silently disarmed every FK declaration; one faults test noticed. `Migrate` now
  enforces foreign keys itself (set before `Up`, since SQLite ignores the pragma
  inside a transaction). `journal_mode` and `busy_timeout` stay the opener's.
- **Python.** `db.py` no longer reads `schema.sql`; it shells out to a new
  `endless-go event migrate`, ~15ms per fresh database. A freshly built
  database must not then enter the legacy `_migrate` ladder, which backs up
  before it short-circuits — that bug was introduced and fixed in-session.
- **sqlc.** Mike plans to adopt sqlc after the Go port. Ran sqlc 1.31.1 against
  the migration directory: the only statement in the whole schema it could not
  parse was `minimizer_evals.ties` (TIES is reserved in its SQLite grammar).
  Quoted in `schema.sql` and the baseline; sqlc now models all 38 structs.
  FTS5 table columns are not modelled, so FTS queries stay hand-written.
  Constraints recorded on E-2021.
- **Ledger shape.** The real ledger does not match its own version 1: a
  pre-rename `tasks.status` default of `'needs_plan'`, a drifted
  `tasks_updated_at` trigger, `tasks.focus_id`, and 11 leftover tables from
  removed features (two of them from change files recorded as applied whose
  DROPs never took effect). Recorded on E-2020, whose version check cannot be a
  shape comparison as a result.

## Verification as shipped

`verify.sh` only — a `verify.toml` beside it would suppress the script (the
runner treats a manifest as winning). Check 5 is scoped to the construction
path: `db.py` still holds DDL in the legacy ladder, which is E-2158's to delete.
The plan's assertions 4 (template hash) and 6 (`_schema_version` and
`apply-change` gone) are not in this suite: the first was not built and the
second moved to E-2158.

# Plan — an explicit DB context, and an answer that says which one

Two halves of one omission: the context can be GUESSED, and the answer never
says which one it used. Half 1 removes the guess; half 2 states the answer.

## 1. endless-go stops guessing

`monitor.SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox()` and its unconditional call in
`cmd/endless-go/main.go`'s startup path are DELETED, not gated. With no caller
left, `setDetectedContextDir` goes with it, and `dbContextFromFlag` collapses
into `dbContextDir != ""` — every context is a flag's now, so the
two-variable split that existed to tell a flag from a guess has nothing left to
tell apart.

`guardWorktreeDBContext` is unchanged. It already refuses when no explicit
context exists inside a self-dev worktree, and it already sits at the single
`DB()` entry point, so it covers every binary that opens the database
including future ones. It stopped firing because detection satisfied it; with
detection gone it fires again. Nothing about the gate was wrong.

`worktreeDBContextRefusal`'s wording changes: it currently says 'Invoke
through the endless CLI with --db main|sandbox, which threads --config-dir to
this binary', which stops being true once endless-go takes --db itself.

## 2. What `--db` means on endless-go

`--db main|sandbox`, consumed before any subcommand body, replacing
`ConsumeDBContextFlag`'s `--config-dir`.

  - `main` → the main config dir.
  - `sandbox` → this worktree's sandbox dir, refused when cwd is not inside a
    self-dev worktree, exactly as Python's `apply_db_choice` already refuses it.

The subtle part, stated so it is not re-litigated later: `--db sandbox` still
reads cwd, because cwd is what says WHICH worktree's sandbox. That is not the
guess coming back. The flag grants permission to open a database; cwd supplies
the address of the one permitted. What is being removed is cwd granting the
permission.

Subcommands that open no database — `task-status`, `session-state`,
`markdown`, `template` — do not accept `--db`; an unknown flag there is a
usage error, as today.

## 3. `--config-dir` retires

Every current caller moves to `--db`, and the ones that genuinely target a
throwaway directory move to `--db-dir <path>`, which keeps an escape without
keeping a second spelling of the normal case.

Note while auditing: `main_config_dir()` is `Path.home()/.config/endless`, so
it FOLLOWS $HOME even though it deliberately ignores $XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Any
caller that already runs under a temp HOME — the verify runner does — is
therefore served by plain `--db main` and needs no escape at all. Decide
per call site rather than converting them all to `--db-dir` by reflex; the
escape is for callers that must name a directory WITHOUT owning the process
environment, chiefly Go tests using `t.TempDir()`.

## 4. Every read AND WRITE states what answered it

One rule, so the three cases below are a rule and not a list:
ANNOUNCE WHAT THE INVOCATION RESOLVED, WHEN IT COULD HAVE RESOLVED OTHERWISE.

  - The DATABASE, in a self-dev project: ALWAYS. Either database could have
    been right on any invocation, so there is no case where the answer was
    never in doubt.
  - The PROJECT, downstream (non-self-dev): ONLY when the resolved project is
    not the one enclosing cwd — a `--project` flag, a session binding, or a
    cwd outside any registered project. With one database and usually one
    project, always-on is repetition, and repetition where nothing varies is
    how a line stops being read.
  - PINNED-IN-CODE contexts: NEVER. See §5 — a pin is not a resolution.

Surfaces:

  - MACHINE formats (`--json`, `--tsv`): a field in the payload. Per-row for
    array payloads (non-breaking — `list-live`'s rows already carry
    `project_id`), once at top level for object payloads.
  - The AGENT-FACING output mode and HUMAN output: in-band on stdout. Where a
    header already names the project — `session list`'s
    `Sessions — project: probe` — the database joins it there rather than
    taking a line of its own. (That mode's flag is `--llm` at the time of
    writing and is being renamed to `--agent` by a concurrent task; this plan
    depends on the mode, not on its spelling. Use whichever name is in the tree
    when this is implemented.)
  - WRITES announce as well as reads. E-1429's founding incident was a WRITE —
    a test `endless task add` that landed in the real ledger as E-1425 — and a
    write to the wrong database is the damaging case, where a wrong read only
    misleads. A mutating command names the database alongside what it changed.

NOT on stderr, deliberately, departing from `rowcap.echo_footer`: that footer
is prose COMMENTARY ABOUT an answer and would corrupt a payload, whereas the
store a result came from is DATA ABOUT THE RESULT and belongs in it. The
analysis records why stderr loses against an agent specifically.

## 5. The exemption

Contexts PINNED IN CODE announce nothing: the hook (`ForceRealDB`), and
`tmux`, `session-status` and `project-status` (`PinMainDB`). If the caller
could not have influenced the choice there is nothing to disambiguate, and the
tmux status line has no room for it. This is §4's rule, not an exception to it.

## 6. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-1668/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit: `internal/monitor` (the gate and its truth table),
   `internal/sessionquerycmd`, and the Python suite.
2. THE INCIDENT, as a regression test. From inside a worktree, using main's
   binary: `endless-go session-query list-live --project-root <main>` with no
   `--db` must REFUSE, naming the remedy. The same call with `--db main` must
   return main's rows. That single pair is the whole of half 1 — it is the
   exact command that silently answered from the sandbox.
3. `SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox` is absent from the tree; no call site remains.
4. No `--config-dir` survives outside the `--db-dir` escape.
5. Provenance, reads: a `--json` read carries the database and project; the
   same read under `--db main` and `--db sandbox` reports different values,
   from a seeded throwaway pair so the difference is checkable rather than
   asserted.
6. Provenance, writes: a `task add` against a seeded sandbox names the
   sandbox in its confirmation. This is E-1425's incident, inverted into a test.
7. The downstream rule: with a single non-self-dev project, a read from inside
   its checkout prints NO project line, and the same read with `--project`
   naming another does.
8. The exemption holds: the tmux status line's bytes are unchanged.

## 7. Not in scope

  - Python's `--db` requirement. It already refuses without the flag inside a
    self-dev worktree; this task changes nothing there.
  - E-1429's gate design. It was right; it was defeated.
  - Renaming the agent-facing output flag. A concurrent task owns `--llm` →
    `--agent`; this one consumes whatever it lands.
## 8. Decided during implementation

Three departures from §4 as written, recorded here so a reviewer meets them in
the plan rather than discovering them in the diff.

**`--tsv` carries nothing.** §4 said machine formats carry a field, naming
`--json` and `--tsv`. `endless sql` is the only `--tsv` surface, its rows are
the columns of arbitrary SQL, and it emits no header row — so the only thing a
"field" could mean there is a trailing column on every row, which silently
changes what every `cut -fN` and `while read` consumer sees. Owner's call,
2026-09-16.

**An array payload is WRAPPED, not tagged per row.** §4 said per-row, on the
grounds that a new envelope "is a breaking change to every consumer". Measured,
that was 4 Python call sites, 11 test assertions and no external consumer — all
in this repo and updatable in the same change. Per-row was wrong on three
counts besides: it said nothing at all for an EMPTY result, which is precisely
the shape the founding incident took; it repeated one identical object once per
row; and it left Endless with two JSON shapes for one question when
`session-status` and `project-status` had been returning `{…, "rows": [...]}`
all along. The wrap is unconditional, so the shape never varies. Owner's call,
2026-09-16.

**The in-band line is one trailing line from one shared function, not folded
into each command's header.** §4 illustrated the rule with `session list`'s
`Sessions — project: probe`, the database joining it there. The trace is instead
written by the root group's result callback, so every command has it and a new
one cannot omit it. Where §4's both-ends intent applies — the agent-facing
renders — a matching leading copy is emitted at the top of each, byte-identical
to the trailing one, on E-2097's rule.

**The Go layer announces the DATABASE only; the PROJECT half lives in Python.**
§4's project bullet fires downstream, and downstream `endless-go` is Python's
helper rather than anything a user types. Threading a resolved project name
through every internal verb would have put the fact where nobody reads it.

### Two flaws this work exposed rather than caused

`sessionquerycmd.TestTaskReport_BinaryEmitsFacts` asserted "the child E-12 is
off the wire" as `strings.Contains(out, "12")` over the whole payload. Any "12"
anywhere satisfied it — a timestamp, a row count — and once the payload carried
a `t.TempDir()` path, whose random digits contain "12" about one run in ten, the
test became intermittently red. Now asserted against the decoded task-fact keys.

The machine-format suppression read `sys.argv`. `click.testing.CliRunner` passes
its arguments to `Command.main` directly and leaves `sys.argv` as pytest's, so
the scan was right in production and silently wrong under test — surfacing only
as test-order-dependent noise. It now takes argv as an argument, from
`DBAwareGroup.main`, which already pre-scans it for `--db`.

## 9. Revisit — output another program takes in

Reopened after landing. §4 kept the trace out of `--json` and `--tsv` and
appended it to everything else, which missed the commands that print a payload
with no flag at all: a value meant for `$(...)`, or shell code meant for `eval`.

What that broke, as reproduced:

  - `session cd --target worktree`: shell-init captures it into `$wt` and tests
    `[ -d "$wt" ]`. A two-line path fails that test and `_endless_run` falls
    back to the global `endless` instead of the worktree's — silently.
  - `worktree for-task`: the guide's own `cd "$(endless worktree for-task <id>)"`
    failed.
  - `session use`, `session id`, `worktree sandbox`: the value carried the line.

The report that reopened this attributed `esu`'s failure to zsh running
`# db: main` as a command without `interactivecomments`. That mechanism did not
reproduce on zsh 5.9 — `eval` honours the comment with the option off — but the
fix does not depend on it: nothing is appended to that output any more.

**Fix.** Declared per command: `<function>.stdout_is_captured = True` in
`cli.py`, beside the command the way `governing_setting` is, honoured in one
place (`AgentAwareCommand.invoke`). Marked: `shell-init`, `session use`,
`session forget`, `session cd`, `session id`, `task id`, `worktree for-task`,
`worktree sandbox`, `db path`. Declared rather than detected because nothing at
run time can tell output captured to be READ from output captured to be RUN — an
agent's shell is not a terminal either, and it is meant to see the line.

`tests/test_captured_output.py` does not trust that list. It scans shell-init
and the docs for `$(endless …)`, resolves each capture against the real command
tree, and fails on any command left unmarked — verified by removing
`shell-init`'s mark and watching it fail naming the four files that capture it.
The first enumeration of these commands used a regex that expected two words
after `endless` and missed `shell-init`, which is why the test resolves against
the tree instead.

**Found beside it.** `endless jobs` and `endless errors` pass `endless-go`'s
stdout straight through and then announce for themselves, and §4's Go wiring
had `jobs` and `errors` announce as well, so the line printed twice. The Go
`Echo` calls are removed; `internal/dbprovenance`'s package doc already stated
that commands Python shells out to keep their output clean of the line.

## The real ledger and schema version 1

E-2019 landed and the ledger is recorded at goose version 1. Measured then, the ledger did NOT match what version 1 declares: a pre-rename `tasks.status` default of 'needs_plan', a `tasks_updated_at` trigger missing its no-op-write guard, an unused `tasks.focus_id`, 11 tables left by removed features (two of them from change files recorded as applied whose DROPs never took effect), and 5 orphaned rows.

That was cleaned up by hand on 2026-09-17, deliberately with no task (Mike's call: data cleansing needs no record). Backups taken before each step are in ~/.config/endless/backups/. Measured after, against a database freshly built from schema.sql:

- Objects: identical set. Nothing extra, nothing missing.
- Columns, types, defaults and foreign keys: identical on every table.
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`: 0 violations. `integrity_check`: ok.
- Still different, both cosmetic: column ORDER on tasks, decisions, task_landings and errors (ALTER-appended rather than declared order), and `session_statuses_session_recent_idx` spelled `(session_id asc, created_at desc)` rather than `(session_id, created_at DESC)` — the same index.

- schema.Migrate(db) is the single way a database acquires its schema (monitor.DB, the sandbox seeder, the ledger projector, tests, and Python via `endless-go event migrate`).

# Plan — every refusal and warning says whether the agent may continue alone

## The rule (Mike, 2026-09-17)

**An agent reports a refusal or warning to the user ONLY when it cannot continue
without input from the user.** Everything else is NO-REPORT.

In particular, a message of the shape "you must do X instead of Y" is NO-REPORT:
the agent calls the command again doing X. Nothing about that needs the user, and
relaying it spends the attention the guardrail exists to save.

This replaces the earlier test in this task's analysis ("after the agent complies,
does the user's outcome differ?"). That test asked about outcomes; this one asks
the only question that decides whether a human is needed, and it is stricter.

Consequence: NO-REPORT is the overwhelming majority. REPORT is the exception, and
every REPORT site should be able to name the decision only the user can make.

Examples:

| Message | Class | Why |
|---|---|---|
| analysis contains an absolute path | NO-REPORT | rewrite it project-relative and retry |
| description over 1024 chars | NO-REPORT | move the long form to --analysis and retry |
| title verb not allowed for this task type | NO-REPORT | pick an allowed verb and retry |
| refusing to remove a worktree | REPORT | removal is the user's act, not the agent's |
| status transition not reachable | NO-REPORT when a legal path exists, else REPORT | classify per site |

## Explicit, never defaulted

Every refusal and warning site carries an explicit classification. There is no
default. A site without one fails the build.

That is the point, not a convenience: a default in either direction is a
classification nobody made. Default-to-report reproduces today's noise;
default-to-silent eventually swallows a genuine blocker. Refusing to build forces
the decision at the moment someone writes the message, when the answer is obvious.

## Scope

**Refusals and warnings, in Python AND Go, fully.**

- Python: `click.ClickException`, `click.UsageError`, and warnings echoed with
  `err=True`. Counted 2026-09-15: 423 raises, 91 warning echoes.
- Go: every user-facing stderr refusal or warning. Counted: 295 stderr writes and
  177 error sentinels (overlapping, and not all user-facing — the inventory decides
  which are).

**Why Go fully, not just where an agent reads it directly:** E-1063 is migrating the
whole CLI surface to Go, with one binary named `endless` as the end state. Python is
transitional. A classification built only on the Python side would be discarded by
the port, and every refusal would have to be classified a second time. The Go side
is the destination, so the mechanism has to exist there.

## The mechanism, per side

**Python — already built, almost unused.** `agent_help.agent_facing()` detects an
agent audience automatically through `agent_env.present()` — no flag for the agent
to remember — and `agent_help.agent_error()` (E-2097) already shapes a refusal
differently for that audience. It has exactly ONE caller against 423 raise sites.
The directive rides on that seam.

Note this is NOT `--llm`. `--llm` is a per-command listing flag on 14 commands, and
Click's exception rendering never consults it, so a refusal could never see it.

**Go — does not exist.** There is no agent-audience detection and no refusal-shaping
helper. The follow-on work builds the Go equivalent of both, reading the same
environment `agent_env` reads, so the two sides cannot disagree about who is
listening.

## The E-1063 port freeze

E-1063 settles that once its port starts, no new Python work lands in the files
being ported — `task_cmd`, `cli`, `worktree_cmd`, `session_cmd` — and anything
still open is re-filed against the Go implementation. E-1063 is underway.

The follow-on todo must check whether that freeze is in force before touching those
four files. If it is, their sites are classified in the inventory (the decision is
still needed) but APPLIED on the Go side as they port, not patched into Python.

## What this research task produces

It changes no code.

1. **The inventory** — every user-facing refusal and warning on both sides, each
   with its class (REPORT / NO-REPORT) and, for every REPORT, the decision only the
   user can make. A site whose class depends on runtime state (the status
   transition above) is marked per-site with the condition, not averaged.
2. **The enforcement design** — how the build refuses an unclassified site on each
   side. Likely a test that walks the raise and stderr sites and requires each to
   go through the classifying helper; the research names the exact shape.
3. **Filed todo task(s)** to apply it — split by side if that is the honest shape,
   respecting the E-1063 freeze.
4. **An outcome** stating the counts, the REPORT list in full (it should be short),
   and anything that did not fit the rule.

## Verification

Research deliverable, reviewed by reading: the outcome names every REPORT site with
its user decision; the NO-REPORT count and the REPORT count sum to the inventory;
the enforcement design is concrete enough to implement; and the follow-on todo
exists, is linked, and cites the E-1063 freeze state it found.

## Scope

Delete the per-ticket change-file mechanism now that goose owns the schema:

- internal/schema/changes/ -- 38 files (15 .go, 23 .sql) plus the runner package, ~2,700 lines.
- The _schema_version table, through a NEW migration, 00002, which drops it — the first real forward migration. Remove its declaration from schema.sql in the same change; TestMigrate_MatchesSchemaSQL fails if only one of the two moves. Never edit 00001_baseline.sql to do this: the real ledger is already recorded at version 1, so editing the baseline would change nothing there and would make every fresh database disagree with it. (Corrected 2026-09-17: an earlier version of this analysis said to edit the baseline.)
- `endless-go event apply-change`, `endless db apply-change`, event_bridge.apply_change.
- db.py's dead legacy migrator: _migrate, _migrate_v2/v3/v5/v6, _should_auto_migrate, the ENDLESS_AUTO_MIGRATE environment variable, and the _has_table/_has_column helpers that serve only them. Its own docstring says it was slated for removal in E-894 Phase 5, and internal/monitor/migrate.go -- the thing that was to replace it -- was deleted by E-1459. It short-circuits at PRAGMA user_version >= 6 and the real ledger is at 12, so it does nothing there. It is NOT inert elsewhere, and it is a PRODUCT problem rather than a tidy-up: nothing in the ladder ever sets user_version above 5, and every database Go builds starts at 0 — every sandbox, and every fresh install on someone else's machine. Such a database takes the whole ladder, preceded by a _backup_db() attempt (throttled to one per 60s), on every Python connect, forever. (Corrected 2026-09-17: an earlier version said the backup runs before the short-circuit test; it runs after it, and the effect is as described here.)

## The one real design step

E-2088 landed 2026-09-16 (901e589) and built cmd/endless-migrate around change FILES: `endless-migrate apply <change-file>`, invoked once per changed file by `worktree land` at Step 5.5, with the file list computed at Step 4.6 and the executable built by `just migrate-bin` in between. Under goose there are no change files to enumerate.

So the executable's subcommand becomes `up`, and the land's question changes from "which change files does this branch add" to "does this branch carry a migration the database has not got" -- schema.LatestVersion() (what the binary carries) compared against the database's recorded version, rather than a directory walk. internal/schemachange is then either deleted outright or reduced to whatever `up` still needs; the `.go` change runner goes with the change files it served.

Do not lose what E-2088 established while reworking it: the build-then-apply ordering (build at 4.6 while base is still untouched, apply at 5.5 between the ff-merge and the record), a build failure aborting with nothing merged and nothing migrated, and an apply failure producing the post-merge message that says re-run rather than restore.

## What E-2019 already verified for this task

internal/schemachange/executable_test.go asserts `go list -deps ./cmd/endless-migrate` links only dbcontext + schemachange + the cmd -- the property that a migration tool carries no code expecting a schema. internal/schema imports nothing but stdlib and github.com/pressly/goose/v3, so it satisfies that property as-is and needs no restructuring. It should REPLACE internal/schemachange in the allowlist, not be added beside it: the test's own rule is that the allowlist is never widened, and once change files are gone schemachange has nothing left to do. (Corrected 2026-09-17: an earlier version said the allowlist simply gains it.)

## Constraint

schema.sql must survive this task. It is still the readable artifact, and E-2021 is what turns it into a generated one; deleting it here leaves it deleted and unreplaced. Deleting only its _schema_version declaration is correct and sufficient.

   environment the harness sets (`CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`,
   `AI_AGENT`). This is the path an agent takes without doing anything, and Endless
   already uses it in many places.
2. **`--agent` was passed.** The token-efficient output flag that superseded `--llm`
   (which is retired, and survives only as a pointer to `--agent`).
3. **`--agent-view` was passed** — a human asking to see what an agent sees.

A human at a terminal with none of these sees today's message unchanged.

## The mechanism, per side

**Python — the seam exists, with one gap.** `agent_help.agent_facing()` is the
single place that answers "is an agent reading this?", and `agent_help.agent_error()`
(E-2097) already shapes a refusal for that audience. Two problems:

- `agent_facing()` is `agent_env.present() or _AGENT_VIEW` — it honours the
  environment and `--agent-view` but NOT `--agent`. Trigger 2 above has to be added
  there, in the one place, not at each call site.
- `agent_error()` has exactly ONE caller against 423 raise sites.

**Go — detection exists, the helper does not.** `internal/agentenv.Present()` already
answers the audience question (4 callers). What Go lacks is the equivalent of
`agent_error()`: nothing shapes a refusal or warning for an agent. The follow-on
builds that helper on top of `agentenv.Present()` plus Go's reading of `--agent`, so
both sides answer the audience question the same way.

## Sequencing with E-1063

E-1063 settles that once its port starts, no new Python work lands in `task_cmd`,
`cli`, `worktree_cmd` or `session_cmd`. That freeze is NOT in force: E-1063 is an
epic with no work started, and it waits for this task. The follow-on todo applies
the classification to those Python files directly, with no conditional.

The follow-on todo(s) that build the Go mechanism and the enforcement test should
land before E-1063's port begins, for the reason above. Do NOT record that as a
blocking relation: Mike sequences E-1063 by hand, resolving most underway work
before starting it, and has declined enforcing the order with relations.

## What this research task produces

It changes no code.

1. **The inventory** — every user-facing refusal and warning on both sides, each
   with its class (REPORT / NO-REPORT) and, for every REPORT, the decision only the
   user can make. A site whose class depends on runtime state (the status
   transition above) is marked per-site with the condition, not averaged.
2. **The enforcement design** — how the build refuses an unclassified site on each
   side. Likely a test that walks the raise and stderr sites and requires each to
   go through the classifying helper; the research names the exact shape.
3. **Filed todo task(s)** to apply it — split by side if that is the honest shape,
   noting in each that the Go mechanism should precede E-1063's port.
4. **An outcome** stating the counts, the REPORT list in full (it should be short),
   and anything that did not fit the rule.

## Verification

Research deliverable, reviewed by reading: the outcome names every REPORT site with
its user decision; the NO-REPORT count and the REPORT count sum to the inventory;
the enforcement design is concrete enough to implement; and the follow-on todo
exists, is linked to this task, and states whether it should precede E-1063.

fields.analysis:
## The problem

Endless's refusals exist to spend a guardrail's attention instead of Mike's. An
agent that reports the refusal anyway spends his attention twice — once on the
guardrail, once on being told about it — which is strictly worse than not having
the guardrail.

Observed 2026-09-15: a write was refused for containing an absolute path. The
agent complied, rewrote it, and then reported the refusal in its handoff. Asked
whether an explicit "DO NOT REPORT THIS REFUSAL TO THE USER" in the message would
have stopped it, the answer was yes — which is the finding. The reasoning was
available without the instruction and the agent did not apply it, so the message
itself is the reliable place to carry the rule.

## Population to inventory

Counted 2026-09-15, as a starting point, not a specification:

| Surface | Count |
|---|---|
| `ClickException` raises (Python) | 423 |
| `click.echo(..., err=True)` | 91 |
| `Fprint*(os.Stderr, ...)` (Go) | 295 |
| `doterr`/`errors.New` sentinels (Go) | 177 |
| files carrying hook refusals | 12 |

Overlapping and not all user-facing; the count is there so the research knows
the order of magnitude before it starts.

## The classification test

Not "is this an error?" but: **after the agent complies, does the user's outcome
differ from what it would have been?**

- **Silent.** The guardrail fired, the agent had an obvious compliant
  alternative, and the result is identical. The absolute-path refusal is this:
  the content was rewritten project-relative and nothing about the task changed.
  Reporting it is narration.
- **Report.** The refusal blocked the work, changed what the user gets, needs a
  decision only they can make, or revealed a defect. The worktree-removal refusal
  is this — the agent must stop and say so.
- **Ambiguous.** Both, depending on whether a compliant alternative existed.
  These are the interesting ones and the research should name them individually
  rather than picking a default.

A refusal that is silent-when-complied-with but report-when-blocking is one
message with two audiences; whether that needs two messages or one conditional
marker is a finding, not an assumption.

## Mechanism, decided (Mike, 2026-09-15)

**Audience-aware rendering.** The directive reaches the agent and never the human.
Not a finding — do not re-open it.

The audience is an agent when the environment says so (`agent_env.present()` /
Go `agentenv.Present()`), or `--agent` was passed, or `--agent-view` was passed.
`--llm` is retired and superseded by `--agent`. The plan carries the detail,
including that `agent_facing()` does not yet honour `--agent`.

Rejected: literal directive text in the message (prose an agent may paraphrase, and
every human reads an instruction addressed to someone else); and a separate
machine-readable marker (a second audience mechanism beside the one that exists).

## Deliverable

The inventory with each user-facing refusal classified silent / report /
ambiguous, the recommended mechanism, and then a FILED todo task to apply it.
This task does not change code.

# Plan — one freshly built endless-go for every Python test

## The problem, measured

`just test` never builds. Python tests that run `endless-go` exercise whatever
binary they find, and in E-1917's worktree that was a copy of main's — producing
a bogus "tasks has 19 columns but 18 values" failure.

Measured before planning, by moving `bin/endless-go` aside and running the full
suite: 5 tests fail (all in `test_template_materialize.py`), 2 SKIP silently,
3456 pass. That is a FLOOR. A test that runs a STALE binary still passes, and a
stale binary is the E-1917 incident exactly.

The Python tests do not resolve the binary one way. They resolve it five ways,
and only one of them builds:

  1. `conftest.isolated_env` (autouse, so every test) prepends `<checkout>/bin`
     to PATH. Nothing builds what is there.
  2. `test_template_materialize._bin()` hard-codes `<checkout>/bin/endless-go`
     by absolute path. Bypasses PATH entirely; fails when absent.
  3. `test_land_conflict.ENDLESS_GO` hard-codes the same path, and `skipif`s
     when it is absent — silent skip when missing, stale when present.
  4. `test_guide_conditionals` PREFERS `bin/endless-go` whenever it exists, falls
     back to PATH, and builds only as a last resort — despite a docstring saying
     "a guard that silently skips … is not a guard".
  5. `test_default_branch_parity.endless_go` builds from this checkout. Correct,
     and the only one that is.

So a PATH-only fix would not have fixed the five tests exposed today: they
reach the binary by absolute path.

## Decisions (owner, 2026-09-17)

  - Research AND fix, in this task. Retyped research → todo.
  - Measure the real count, not just the floor (§2).
  - GLOBAL, not scoped to the tests §2 finds. E-1063 turns Python commands into
    shims over `endless-go` one at a time, so the set of tests that shell out
    GROWS through the port. A hand-maintained scope would need every newly
    shimmed command added, which is the forgettable-list failure again.
  - PRODUCT: no change. `verify.toml`'s `setup` is already where a project
    declares its own build, and Endless cannot know a downstream build graph.
  - Worth doing ahead of E-1063. E-2084 puts E-1921 first because "the port's
    whole safety net is 'the tests pass'".

## 1. One build site

A session-scoped fixture in `tests/conftest.py`, `endless_go_bin`, builds
`./cmd/endless-go` once into `tmp_path_factory` and returns the path. It is the
existing `test_default_branch_parity.endless_go` fixture, MOVED rather than
copied — reuse before creation.

  - Build failure fails the session loudly (`pytest.fail` with the compiler's
    stderr). It must never fall back to `bin/` or PATH: a fallback is the stale
    binary this task removes.
  - `go` missing from PATH fails with a message naming it.

## 2. Measure the real count first

Before changing any resolver, run the full suite once with every route to the
binary instrumented:

  - a logging `endless-go` shim FIRST on PATH, and
  - `<checkout>/bin/endless-go` temporarily replaced by the same shim (the real
    binary moved aside and restored by trap), since routes 2–4 bypass PATH.

The shim appends `$PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST` and its argv to a log, then execs the
real binary. pytest sets that variable per test and subprocesses inherit it, so
every invocation is attributed to the test that caused it.

The outcome records: the number of tests that invoke the binary, by route, and
any route not in the five above. If §2 finds a sixth route, §3 covers it.

## 3. Point every route at the one build

  - Route 1: `isolated_env` prepends `endless_go_bin`'s directory instead of
    `<checkout>/bin`. It stays autouse, so every test gets a current binary
    without anyone listing it — the global decision.
  - Routes 2, 3, 4: replace each test's own resolver with the fixture. Route 3's
    `skipif` is DELETED: a test that silently skips when the binary is missing
    proves nothing in the one environment where it matters.
  - Route 5: uses the fixture it donated.

Also corrected, because they now describe the wrong mechanism:
`isolated_env`'s comment (it names `endless-event` and a sibling-worktree
symlink) and `test_epic_cmd.py`'s docstring (it says event emission runs through
the binary on PATH; with the binary removed those tests pass).

Not touched: `just test-go`. Go's `TestMain` in `eventcmd` and `sessionquerycmd`
already builds per package and is correct by construction.

## 4. How this ends — E-1063

The fixture carries no weight past the port and needs no migration. E-2084
settled that "the suite the port leaves behind is Go's" and lists the pytest
isolation fixtures as subsumed; this fixture is deleted with `tests/`. The one
rule a ported test must keep is Go's existing one: use the `TestMain`-built
binary, never `bin/endless-go`.

## 5. Costs, measured

  - One build per pytest SESSION: 1.4 s with a warm Go cache, 8.1 s cold.
  - The verify runner substitutes HOME, so GOCACHE starts cold there. Each
    `uv run pytest` gate in a suite is its own session and pays ~8 s.
  - A Go compile error now fails the Python suite too. Deliberate: testing
    Python against a binary that no longer matches its source is the bug.

No mitigation for the cold cache is in scope.

## 6. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-1921/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

  1. Fail-fast gate: the tests this task changes, plus the full Python suite.
  2. THE INCIDENT, inverted into a test. Replace `<checkout>/bin/endless-go`
     with a POISONED binary (a script that exits 99), and put another poisoned
     `endless-go` first on PATH. Run the previously exposed files —
     `test_template_materialize.py`, `test_land_conflict.py`,
     `test_guide_conditionals.py` — and require them to PASS with zero skips.
     Restore by trap. That single run is the whole claim: neither `bin/` nor
     PATH can influence which binary a test runs.
  3. Remove `<checkout>/bin/endless-go` entirely and require the same files to
     pass with zero skips (the silent-skip route is gone).
  4. Structure: no test file resolves `bin/endless-go` itself, and the only
     `go build` of `./cmd/endless-go` under `tests/` is `endless_go_bin`.
  5. The count from §2 is recorded in the outcome, and the suite asserts the
     instrumented run found no route outside those the fixture covers.

# Plan — rebuild project monitor and project status around tasks

Specified by Mike in conversation on 2026-09-15, with `project monitor` open in
front of him. This replaces the display E-1976 shipped; it is not a tweak to it.

Explicitly an interim shape. Mike expects to replace it with a scrolling TUI
before long, and wants to live with this one to learn what he actually needs.
Build what is specified here and stop; do not optimise past it.

## The shape

One tmux pane holds the whole of `project monitor`, with the CLI pane beneath it
(the existing two-pane layout, unchanged). Inside that pane, THREE lists, in this
order, with NO separator rows and no headers between them:

1. **urgent** — `phase = 'urgent'`, non-terminal. UNTRUNCATED.
2. **epics** — `type = epic`, `phase IN ('now','next')`, non-terminal.
   UNTRUNCATED.
3. **everything else** — non-epic, `phase IN ('now','next')`, non-terminal.
   The ONLY truncated list: it takes whatever pane height remains, and grows
   when the user grows the terminal.

Each task appears ONCE, in the highest list it qualifies for: an urgent epic is
in list 1, never also in list 2; an epic is never in list 3.

Separators are unnecessary because the rows identify themselves — list 1 carries
the urgent phase glyph, list 2 carries the epic type letter. Mike may revisit
this; do not add separators pre-emptively.

## Ordering

All three lists sort reverse-chronologically.

`--sort` on BOTH `project monitor` and `project status`, taking `updated`
(default) or `id`. Mike was undecided between them and wants to try both in use,
which is the flag's whole purpose — do not pick one and drop the other.

## `project status` does not truncate

Not the third list, not anything. It is the surface for seeing everything,
including what the monitor cannot fit, and Mike expects to pipe it through grep
routinely to find tasks the monitor is not showing.

`--later` shows ONLY `phase = 'later'` tasks — the phase the other views exclude.

## Rows

Reuse `session status`'s row rendering. It is well optimised for an experienced
reader and there is no reason to invent a second format; share the code.

Changes for this context:

- **Drop the time/age column.** It is not useful here, and — the reason that
  matters more — it changes every tick, so the frame differs on every repaint and
  the pane moves constantly in the corner of the eye. Removing it makes motion
  mean something: the pane only redraws when the row set actually changes.
- **Drop the session-relative glyphs**: `●` (this session's task), `↑` (parent),
  `↩` (from/spawner). They describe a viewing session, and there is none here.
- **Keep the action glyph.** E-1976's error was GROUPING by it, not showing it.
- **Keep the phase glyph on every row**, including in the urgent list where it is
  technically redundant — for vertical alignment, and because it is what the eye
  is used to.
- Keep the type letter, the id, and the title.

## Sessions are consulted, never displayed

No session appears as a row. But a task's row DOES reflect whether a live session
is on it: `⟳` for `underway` with a live session, `◷` for `underway` without —
the distinction `session status` already draws, and the only signal that claimed
work has stalled.

E-2091's `prompted` state extends this naturally: a task whose live session is
blocked on a permission prompt should wear the `⚠` glyph rather than `⟳`, since
that is the same fact at a higher urgency. STATED EXPLICITLY so it can be
rejected: it follows from "the row reflects a live session" plus the existing
glyph vocabulary, but Mike did not say it in as many words.

## What is removed

- **All session rows**, and with them the "sessions with no task" list that
  prompted this redesign. They were unactionable — three such rows led to
  "Session NNN has no reachable tmux pane" when followed.
- **Idle-session reporting.** tmux window tabs already carry it. Out of scope
  now; Mike may revisit when a TUI can do more.
- **The seven-rank classification as a grouping mechanism** (`waiting`, `verify`,
  `read`, `review`, `orphan`, `idle`, `doing`). The glyphs survive on rows; the
  grouping does not. There is no ordering among statuses that says one matters
  more than another — they are all points in one workflow.
- **The per-rank cap and its fair-share allocation.** One list truncates, by pane
  height alone.
- **`--limit` / `--no-limit`.** Nothing is count-capped any more. This leaves
  `rowcap.limit_options_for` with no caller; remove it too if so, rather than
  leaving a factory nothing builds from.
- **`--all`.** Its meaning was "also include `ready`", which is now included by
  default as a non-terminal status.

Keep `--json` and the fault badge as they are.

## Status filtering was considered and rejected

Measured while planning: list 3 holds 295 tasks for this project — 127
`unplanned`, 92 `submitted`, 38 `unverified`, 25 `ready`, 13 `underway`.

The obvious move is to filter to statuses needing the user specifically. Mike
rejected it (2026-09-15): `session status` carries the per-session detail, this
is the high-level view, and no status is inherently more important than another
because they are all part of one workflow. `unplanned` and `ready` are both
needed now — they may matter less once auto-spawn and auto-planning exist, which
is a reason to revisit later and not to filter now.

The pane running out of room is not a defect to design around. It is the pressure
that gets work demoted to `later`, the same way 20 untruncated epics is the
pressure that gets epics demoted.

## Terminology

Use the names the product uses: `project status` (the snapshot) and `project
monitor` (the live loop), or both commands where a sentence means the pair. E-2153
removed a coined synonym for the two from the tree; this rebuild rewrites most of
the files that cleanup touched, so it is the likeliest place for a new coinage to
appear. Do not introduce one — if something genuinely lacks a name, ask.

## Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-<id>/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit gate: `internal/projectstatuscmd`, `internal/monitor`, and the
   Python suite.
2. The three lists, in order, against a seeded database: an urgent task, an
   urgent epic, a now epic, a next epic, and non-epic tasks across the
   non-terminal statuses. Assert the order and that each task appears exactly
   once.
3. Untruncated means untruncated: seed more urgent tasks and more epics than fit
   a small `--rows` budget and assert every one renders.
4. Only list 3 truncates, and by height: the same row set at two `--rows` values
   yields more list-3 rows at the larger one, with lists 1 and 2 unchanged.
5. `--sort id` and `--sort updated` produce different orders on a fixture built
   so they must (an old task updated recently).
6. `project status` truncates nothing at any `--rows` value, and `--later` shows
   only `later` tasks.
7. No row renders a session: no `ES-` id, and no `●`/`↑`/`↩` glyph, on any
   fixture.
8. A task held by a live session renders `⟳` and the same task with no live
   session renders `◷`.
9. No age column: two renders of an unchanged row set, taken a second apart, are
   byte-identical. This is the repaint-motion property, and asserting it on the
   frame is what keeps it from regressing when a future column carries a clock.
10. No coined term: the rebuilt files carry no name for these views other than
    `project status` and `project monitor`.

A Go test fails the build on any os.Stderr reference outside the package. Convert every lang=go row of docs/research-2026-09-17-refusal-inventory.tsv to its class. Land before E-1063's port so ported refusals are born classified, and before the Python follow-on, which consumes this package's golden rendering and ENDLESS_AUDIENCE contract.
payload.plan:
# Plan — one Go package decides who a refusal is for, and the build refuses any write that skips it

Implements the enforcement design in
`docs/research-2026-09-17-refusal-inventory.md` (Go, Hooks, Rendering,
Cross-process). The rows to convert are the `lang=go` rows of
`docs/research-2026-09-17-refusal-inventory.tsv`: 449 classified
(REPORT 120, NO-REPORT 249, CONDITIONAL 80) plus 15 INFO and 104 EXCLUDED, which
must also route through the package because the check cannot tell them apart.

## Order

Land this BEFORE E-1063's port begins, so every refusal ported into Go is born
classified and the check catches any the port misses. Not recorded as a blocking
relation: E-1063 is sequenced by hand. Land it before the Python follow-on too —
this package owns the golden rendering and the `ENDLESS_AUDIENCE` contract that
Python consumes.

## Build

1. A package (name open; `internal/refusal` in the doc) with class-named
   constructors only — `NoReport(summary, remedy)`, `Report(summary, decision)`,
   `ReportIf(summary, condition, remedy, decision)`, `Fault(err)`, `Warn`,
   `Info`, `Passthrough()` for a child's stderr, `(*Error).Exit(code)`,
   `Block(*Error)` for PreToolUse, and `From(err)` for a generic print site.
2. Audience: `agentenv.Present() || os.Getenv("ENDLESS_AUDIENCE") == "agent"`.
   Hook output takes its audience from the hook event and exit path instead
   (PreToolUse exit 2 / block reason / additionalContext → agent;
   UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart exit 2 and Stop exit 1 → human).
3. Rendering: humans get today's text unchanged. Agents get the E-2097 bracket —
   one verdict line first and last — with the directive inside the verdict line
   (wording in the doc). A REPORT renders the decision and not the bypass.
4. A golden file of rendered verdicts, one per class, asserted here and by the
   Python follow-on.
5. The check: a Go test (`go/parser`) over non-test files in `internal/` and
   `cmd/` that fails on any `os.Stderr` selector outside the package. That covers
   `fmt.Fprint*(os.Stderr`, `cmd.Stderr = os.Stderr`, `log.SetOutput(os.Stderr`,
   and `slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr`. The 3 injected stderr writers become the
   package's own type, which has no `Write`. The failure message states the rule
   and lists the constructors.
6. Logging: move the standard-logger setup out of `hookcmd`'s `init()` (which
   today redirects `log` for EVERY endless-go subcommand) into the package, and
   send it to the log file only.
7. Convert every Go row in the TSV to its class. CONDITIONAL rows of kind
   *state* compute the class at the site; *intent* rows use `ReportIf`; *relay*
   rows use `Passthrough` or classify at the site.
8. While each message is open, fix the Go message defects the doc lists
   (`blockCommitOnMainIfApplicable` names `git commit --no-verify` as the bypass,
   which its own regex blocks; `handlePostToolUse` says "Plan file synced to
   Endless" though that sync no longer happens; `ValidateNoParentCycle` names
   `task move <id> --root` without the `endless` prefix; `templatecmd.Run` prints
   `runRender`'s flag error twice; `bindCmd` and the sandbox "already exists" /
   "stale sandbox directory" errors name the retired `endless-sandbox` binary;
   `refuseRebuildDBConfirm` cites Endless's own task ids;
   `ValidateStatusTransition` cites `docs/status-lifecycle.mmd`, which a foreign
   project does not have).
9. Make the cause reach the site: a failed `.go` schema change reports only
   "exit status 1" because the runner's real reason goes to a stderr the caller
   discards (`schemachange.applyGo`, and `runner.Run`'s `log.Printf` before
   `os.Exit(1)`); carry it in the returned error.

## Decide before implementing (open questions in the doc)

- Q2: trigger 1 recognises only the Claude Code terminal and Desktop; an agent
  in the VS Code extension or the SDK reads as a human.
- Q3: `From(err)` renders an unclassified error as a fault — the one place a
  class is implied. Accept, or require every Run error to be a `*refusal.Error`?
- Q4: warnings the user should act on but that block nothing become inert under
  the rule (doc, *did not fit* item 2) — accept, or give them another channel?

## Verification

- `just test-go` passes, including the new check.
- Temporarily adding `fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "x")` to any package fails the
  check with a message naming the rule.
- With `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli`, an illegal `endless-go event emit` status
  change prints the bracketed verdict with the directive; without it, the text
  is byte-identical to today's.
- `ENDLESS_AUDIENCE=agent` alone produces the agent rendering.

An AST test fails the build on any ClickException/UsageError construction, err=True echo, stderr write or non-zero exit outside the helper. Convert every lang=py row of docs/research-2026-09-17-refusal-inventory.tsv. Lands after E-2159, whose golden rendering it asserts.
